How this volume is built

Every module opens with the idea in plain language, draws it once as a plate you cannot misread, then asks you to produce the answer before it shows you one. Nothing here is marked studied because you clicked it.

The meter in the running head counts one thing only: graded items you answered correctly on the first attempt. It is a diagnostic, not a participation trophy — a low number the night before the exam is the most useful thing this page can tell you.

    ITriage before you read

    Eight questions you answer about yourself, and one rule that turns the answers into a reading order.

    Twenty-five modules sit behind this one, and reading them in printed order is the most expensive route through the volume you can take. Printed order spends the same evening on the objective that carries a fifth of your final and on the objective that carries seven percent of it. So answer eight questions about yourself first — before you read a word about the cloud — and let the instrument on this plate turn those answers into an order you can defend.

    In the margin

    The course does this to you twice on purpose: a self-audit in Session 1 and a post-test in Session 12 over the same eight objectives, so the reading at the end can be laid against the reading at the start.

    Plate 26 re-scores these same eight lights from the record instead of from your feeling.

    Set one light per objective. Green is not “I have heard of it.” Green is: you could stand in front of Marguerite Harlow, who owns Harbor Lane Books and has never used either acronym in her life, and produce the answer cold, in her words, without notes. Amber is: you can pick the right answer out of four but cannot generate it on blank paper. Red is: you would have to look it up. Rate what you can produce, because the exam hands you a stakeholder sentence and asks you to produce.

    Then the second fact, and it has nothing to do with you. The eight objectives are not equally weighted. Virtualization and operations carries about a fifth of a full-course final; storage and sharing carries fifteen percent; the platform objective carries seven. A confidence reading on its own therefore cannot set a reading order, because confidence says nothing about the stakes. Two students, equally shaky, can be in wildly different trouble.

    Exam trap

    Green because you know the acronym. Knowing that RTO measures forward and RPO backward is vocabulary. The exam hands you a clinic manager who never says either word — “closed for a day, but we cannot lose any charting” — and asks which pair she has just given you. That is production, and it is what the light is supposed to report.

    So the rule multiplies. A red light keeps the whole of that objective’s share against you, amber keeps half of it, green keeps none. Call the product exposure. The route is every objective whose exposure is above zero, heaviest first, ties broken toward the earlier objective because the later modules assume the earlier ones. Exposure — not colour, not the order the modules are printed in — is the only number this volume sorts a reading route by.

    Two limits close the rule, and they are read the way you will read every other pair of limits in this course: the stricter one binds. Total carried exposure at or under 10, and no single objective above 5. Put together, they say something blunt and useful — you may walk into the final shaky on the two lightest objectives, SaaS and PaaS, and shaky on nothing heavier than that.

    One thing this audit cannot do is catch you flattering yourself, because you are the only witness to it. An objective you have never opened glows exactly as green as one you have mastered. That is not a flaw to fix on this plate; it is the reason the volume closes with the same eight objectives scored by the record — every graded item, first attempts only — instead of by your feeling about them.

    Set the eight lights on the instrument below. Then, before you commit anything, say out loud which objective you think the rule will open at and set the last dial to it. That call is the only thing here you can be wrong about in an interesting way: it tests whether you have taken on the multiplication or are still ranking by colour.

    The whole rule fits in four lines, and it is worth being able to run it on the back of an envelope in the exam room, where there is no instrument:

    Item 1.1All eightRouting

    A student rates Objective 6 — storage and sharing, fifteen percent of the final — amber, and Objective 3 — PaaS, seven percent — red. Which objective does the route rule open at, and on what ground?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The worst light wins. Ranking by colour throws away half the product. A red light on a light objective can cost you less than an amber on a heavy one, and the exam pays out on share, not on how bad the gap felt.

    • Correct

      Both facts multiplied. 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 against 7 × 1.0 = 7.0. Storage opens first, by 0.5 of the final’s weight, and the rule does not care that the light on it was the better of the two.

    • No

      Printed order mistaken for study order. The volume is sequenced for a first reading. On a second pass, dependency only ever breaks a tie between two equal exposures — it never overturns one.

    • No

      The instrument refused. A self-set light is weak evidence, not an absence of evidence. The cure for weak evidence is the record-scored audit at the end of the volume, not paralysis at the front of it.

    Synthesis: exposure is a product, so its ranking moves when either factor moves — which is why the audit asks for a light per objective rather than “what are you worst at.” The answer to that question is not the answer to “what should I read tonight.” Notice how narrow this call was, 7.5 against 7.0: two exposures that close are one evening’s work in either order, and the rule is a route, not a verdict.

    Item 1.2All eightScoring

    A Harbor Lane Books manager sets Objective 5 — identity — to green because he picks the right answer out of four every time he meets one. Under this volume’s scoring rule, what is wrong with that light?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Recognition counted as production. Four options do most of the work for him: they supply the vocabulary, the shape of a right answer, and three wrong shapes to eliminate. Blank paper supplies none of that, and neither does a client.

    • No

      Format mistaken for faculty. Objective 5 is examined both ways — a written trace of the flow, and selection items alongside it. The defect is not which format he practises; it is which ability he reported.

    • No

      Coverage mistaken for ability. How many items he has opened is a fact about the record, and the closing plate is where the record scores it. A light is a claim about what he could produce today.

    • Correct

      The claim the colour makes. Green says: I could trace the flow, name what the browser carries and what returns over the back channel, with no notes. If he cannot do that unprompted, the honest light is amber.

    Synthesis: this volume scores two different things and neither substitutes for the other. A light is your own claim about what you can generate; the meter in the running head counts graded items answered correctly on the first attempt and nothing else. When the two disagree, believe the meter — then set the light again, which is exactly what the closing plate makes you do.

    Item 1.3All eightLimits

    An audit totals 9.5 of carried exposure, under this volume’s ceiling of 10 — but Objective 7 alone accounts for 6.0 of that total. What does the route rule return?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      Both limits read. 6.0 on one objective is above 5, so the route fails the per-objective limit while passing the total. The stricter limit binds — the same move you will make in Session 9, where the stricter recovery clock sets the architecture.

    • No

      The total hiding the hole. A route can pass on the aggregate and still leave a fifth of the final unproduced. Catching precisely that is why a second limit exists at all; one number cannot see inside itself.

    • No

      Self-audit confused with the record. These lights are set by you and know nothing about which items you have opened. The closing plate is the instrument that reads the record; this one only multiplies what you claim.

    • No

      A limit turned into a feeling. 9.5 is under 10, and a rule you round against when it suits you has stopped being a rule. The route does fail, but it fails on a stated number, for a stated reason.

    Synthesis: two limits, and the answer is never their average. One asks whether the whole estate is safe; the other asks whether any single part of it can sink you on its own. You will meet that shape twice more before the end — in the stricter of two recovery clocks, and in a chain of multiplied availabilities that no single strong link can rescue.

    6 of 6 terms
    S1
    Your own rating of one objective: red for cannot yet produce it, amber for can recognise but not generate it, green for could teach it cold. A claim about production, never about coverage.
    S1
    What a light keeps against you — red 1.0, amber 0.5, green 0. The half of the product you can change tonight.
    S1
    An objective’s share of the final multiplied by its deficit. The only number this volume sorts a reading route by.
    S1
    Every objective with exposure above zero, heaviest first, ties broken toward the earlier objective. An order, not a verdict.
    S1 · S12
    Picking the right answer from four, against generating it on blank paper. The audit scores the second, and so does the client in front of you.
    S1 · S12
    Only your first answer to a graded item moves the meter in the running head. A retry serves a fresh variant to practise on; it cannot repaint a miss.
    Decision rule

    If two objectives feel the same, open the heavier one. A halved twenty beats a whole seven, every time — and if you are ever unsure whether a light should be green or amber, it is amber.

    IIThe objective map

    Eight objectives, twelve sessions, one hundred per cent of a final — drawn once, so nothing you revise is untraceable.

    Eight objectives carry this course. Every plate, bench and drilled item in the rest of this volume answers to exactly one of them, and every one of them answers to a share of one paper. The fastest way to waste a revision pass is to study something that no row of this map carries.

    In the margin

    This is the only module here that is not about cloud computing. It is about where the cloud computing you are revising gets counted.

    See Plate 2 for the whole grid at once.

    Each objective answers three separate questions, and confusing them is the commonest planning error a student makes. Sessions say when the course taught it. Share says how much of one named paper samples it. Mastery proof says what you must be able to do — not recognise, not restate, but perform on an unfamiliar case. A revision plan built on the first two and blind to the third produces a student who can name the four deployment models and still cannot assign one to Rosa's clinic.

    The shape of the map is worth reading before any of its rows. Objectives 5, 6 and 7 — identity, storage and collaboration, and virtualization with its security, recovery and operations tail — take 48 per cent of the full-course final between them. Objective 7 alone takes 20 per cent, the heaviest single row, and yet all four of its sessions (7, 8, 9 and 11) sit past the midterm's reach. Objective 6 takes 15 per cent out of only two sessions, 5 and 6, which makes that pair the densest ground on the map.

    Exam trap

    A share is a fact about one paper. Objective 7's 20 per cent describes the full-course final; on the Weeks 1–2 midterm the same objective appears only as the shared-responsibility line.

    Read the columns too. Session 6 is where three objectives meet — SaaS, identity, and storage and collaboration — so a Session 6 vignette can be marked against any of them, and "we covered that in Session 6" names nothing. Session 12 touches four objectives at once, because migration is not new material; it is the course re-entered through a different door.

    Item 2.1All objectivesMap reading

    Objective 7 carries the largest share of the full-course final, yet every session that teaches it — 7, 8, 9 and 11 — sits after the midterm's reach. What does the map license you to conclude?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      One sweep for two papers. The two papers draw from different halves of the map. The midterm reaches Sessions 1 to 6; the final reaches all twelve, and the difference is not a rounding error — it is the four sessions that carry the heaviest objective in the course.

    • No

      Weight carried across papers. The 20 per cent is a fact about the final's blueprint only. On the midterm this objective shows up as the shared-responsibility line and almost nothing else, because its sessions had not happened yet.

    • Correct

      Both facts read off one map. Sessions say when it was taught; share says how much of a named paper samples it. Put together they say the obvious thing: revise for the paper in front of you, not for the course in general.

    • No

      Weight read as difficulty. A share measures how much of the paper samples an objective, not how hard the material is. Objective 6 takes 15 per cent from two early sessions; nobody would call it the second-hardest thing in the course.

    Synthesis: sessions, share and mastery proof are three independent facts about the same row, and every planning error in this course comes from reading one of them as if it were another. Sessions tell you when, share tells you how much of which paper, and the proof tells you what you must be able to perform.

    Item 2.2All objectivesProof vs topic

    Objective 6 reads: differentiate cloud data-storage solutions and cloud collaboration solutions. Which line is a mastery proof of it — rather than a topic, a restatement, or another objective's proof?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      A proof is a performance. It names the input (how the workload reads and writes), the decision (block, file or object) and the discriminating fact that defends it. Hand it an unfamiliar workload and it still works.

    • No

      The objective restated. An objective is a promise about what you will be able to do; saying it back demonstrates nothing. This is the line students write when they have read the syllabus and not the sessions.

    • No

      Recall mistaken for demonstration. An ordered list survives exactly until the vignette arrives in a different order. The paper never asks for the three types; it hands you three workloads and asks for the assignment.

    • No

      Right proof, wrong objective. That is Objective 7's two-clock rule from Session 9. Filing it here is how a review stops being traceable: the module would claim a row that does not carry it.

    Synthesis: every module in this review closes on a proof of this shape — given a stated situation, make the assignment and defend it with the fact that discriminates. Restatements and ordered lists both feel like knowing, and the paper is built to tell the difference.

    8 of 8 terms
    S1 · S12
    Run the five-trait test on an unfamiliar product and name the trait that fails. "Not cloud" is a classification, not an insult.
    S2 · S6 · S12
    Explain multi-tenancy as a tenant id enforced on every query, and name the two legitimate risks: the noisy neighbour and the vendor-side blast radius.
    S2 · S10
    Apply the practical test — there is no server you can log into — then name the price you pay for it: runtime-version control and lock-in exposure.
    S3 · S7 · S12
    Size a machine from the server's role using the five knobs, then take the fleet as peak divided by per-server green capacity, rounded up, plus one.
    S4 · S6 · S8
    Validate a token the way an app must — issuer, algorithm and signature, time claims, exact audience. Decoding is not validating.
    S5 · S6
    Assign block, file or object from what the workload reads and writes, and hold durability apart from availability using the authorized-delete case.
    S7 · S8 · S9 · S11
    Set the recovery time forward and the recovery point backward, then buy the cheapest tier that satisfies the stricter of the two clocks.
    S10 · S11 · S12
    Rebuild a service's internals, keep the published contract, and break no consumer — then give every system in a portfolio exactly one of the 6 Rs.

    Eight rows, eight proofs. The rest of this volume is those eight lines slowed down, drawn, and drilled — and every module from here on names the row it answers to in its first line, so you can always ask the only question that matters about a paragraph you are reading: which proof does this serve?

    Next Is it cloud at all?
    Objective 1 · Session 1

    IIIIs it actually cloud?

    Five traits decide it, and one failed trait ends the argument. Everything later in this review assumes you can run the test.

    Not every remote server is a cloud. That single sentence is the whole of this module, and it is the discrimination the exam returns to more often than any other, because a student who cannot tell cloud from hosting will misclassify every service model, every deployment model and every bill that follows.

    In the margin

    The course’s anchor image: when you flip a light switch you neither know nor care which plant made the electricity. When you save a photo “to the cloud” you do not know which physical disk in which building holds it — and that is the point. You trade control of hardware for freedom from hardware.

    See Plate 3A for the test applied to three real candidates.

    The cloud is an abstraction, not an address. Somebody still owns racks, cooling, power, guards and spare disks; the abstraction is that none of that reaches you. What makes the arrangement cloud rather than merely somebody else’s computer is the delivery model: on demand, over a network, from a shared pool, elastic in both directions, and metered. Those five conditions are the industry’s standard test, and they are the vocabulary every story problem in this course is graded in.

    Run them in order and stop at the first one that fails. Gate 1, on-demand self-service: you provision it yourself, in minutes, with no purchase order and no technician — ordering a physical server takes weeks. Gate 2, broad network access: it is reachable over standard networks from phones, laptops and other servers; if it only works from one wired terminal in one building, it is not cloud. Gate 3, resource pooling: the provider’s hardware serves many consumers at once, your VM sharing a host with a stranger’s, isolated by virtualization — pooling is why prices are low. Gate 4, rapid elasticity: capacity stretches and shrinks with demand, so that to you it looks unlimited. Gate 5, measured service: usage is metered like electricity, per hour, per gigabyte, per request.

    Exam trap

    “The cloud is a big data center in Virginia.” No. Naming a place answers a different question. The exam wants the abstraction plus the delivery model — on demand, over a network, pay per use — and it will offer you a street address to see whether you take it.

    Missing one gate is disqualifying, and that is a classification rather than an insult. A leased cage in a colocation centre, a fixed virtual private server on a flat annual contract, a well-run in-house hypervisor cluster — all of them are legitimate, sometimes excellent, ways to buy computing. None of them is cloud, which means none of them gives you elasticity or metered economics, and you should stop expecting cloud arguments to apply to them.

    Read the plate as an assay rather than a scorecard. Rosa’s cage and Bayfront’s farm both fail, but they fail at different gates, and the gate is the interesting fact: one is a hardware-ownership problem and the other is a capacity-and-billing problem, and they have completely different fixes. A score of 3 out of 5 tells you almost nothing. “Stops at gate 4” tells you what to buy.

    Item 3.1Objective 1Discrimination

    Rosa runs a 14-person accounting firm in Tampa. Client files sit on one server in a hallway closet and her nephew copies them to a USB drive “most Fridays.” In July a pipe bursts and soaks both. Which characteristic would most directly have prevented the loss?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      A capacity trait asked to do a durability job. Elasticity answers swings in demand, and a 14-person firm’s load is flat. However the storage grew, it grew in the same closet.

    • No

      A billing property mistaken for a safeguard. Metering changes what Rosa pays, not whether the files survive. Nothing about a per-gigabyte invoice puts a second copy anywhere.

    • Correct

      Pooling is what puts the copies in more than one room. Her real failure is that every copy shared one closet. Provider hardware serving many customers keeps redundant copies across devices and, configured properly, across regions.

    • No

      Recovery speed mistaken for prevention. Self-service helps her stand up a replacement after the flood. By then the files are already gone: it prevents delay, not loss.

    Synthesis: the five traits are a test, not a ranking, so “which trait is most impressive” is never the question — “which trait caused this outcome” always is. Elasticity and metering are the standing decoys in a durability story because they are the two traits students find most memorable.

    Once a candidate clears all five gates, the second question is where it lives and who else is on it. Four deployment models answer that, and they are not a quality ranking — they are answers to a trust-boundary question. Public cloud rents shared infrastructure to anyone with a credit card: maximum pooling, minimum cost, fastest start. Private cloud dedicates cloud-style infrastructure to a single organization, on premises or hosted, and trades cost for control. Community cloud is shared by organizations with a common need and a common rulebook — five hospitals splitting one HIPAA-compliant platform. Hybrid is a deliberate combination: sensitive systems stay private while everyday or spiky workloads burst to public. Most real enterprises end up hybrid, which is worth remembering for the capstone.

    Exam trap

    Reaching for community the moment two organizations appear in a stem. Community requires a shared regulatory or mission need. A bank’s marketing site is not a shared regulated workload, and competitors do not co-own a ledger.

    The four deployment models, and the question each one answers
    ModelWho shares the hardwareChosen whenWorked client
    PublicAnyone with a credit cardNo special rule applies; cost and speed dominateTicketBlitz’s web tier
    PrivateOne organization, aloneRegulation or secrecy outranks costClassified defense workloads
    CommunityAllied orgs, one rulebookShared obligations, none able to fund it aloneFive rural hospitals, HIPAA
    HybridBoth, split by workloadRequirements differ inside one organizationCoastal Bank & Trust
    Decision rule

    Cheapest, fastest, no special rules → public. One org, regulation or secrecy dominant → private. Several allied orgs under one rulebook, none able to afford private alone → community. Split requirements inside one organization → hybrid.

    The deployment model never relaxes the five-trait test. A “private cloud” that cannot provision itself, cannot stretch and meters nothing is not a private cloud; it is a server room with a nicer name, which is exactly Bayfront’s farm on Plate 3A. Every model has to pass all five gates on its own side of the boundary — and in a hybrid, both sides do.

    aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abc123 \
  --instance-type t3.small --count 4        # gate 1 in one line: no purchase
                                            # order, no technician, ~90 seconds
# gate 5 is the other half of that line: the meter starts here and stops on
# terminate. Both traits, one command — which is why the exam pairs them.

    Item 3.2Objective 1Model selection

    Coastal Bank & Trust wants a modern public website with spiky seasonal campaigns, but regulators and internal policy require the core banking ledger to run on infrastructure the bank exclusively controls. The CTO wants one coherent strategy, not two disconnected worlds. What should she choose?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      Each workload sent where its requirements point. Control for the regulated ledger, elasticity and low cost for the campaign traffic, and secure networking between them so it is one system rather than two.

    • No

      Community stretched past its definition. Community serves allied organizations under a shared rulebook. Competing banks share a regulator, not a mission — and they do not co-own each other’s ledgers.

    • No

      Compliance treated as negotiable. This bets the banking licence on regulators changing their minds. The requirement is an input to the design, not an obstacle to argue with.

    • No

      Peak capacity bought outright. The bank would own hardware sized for the busiest campaign day and idle it the rest of the year — the exact waste public cloud rents away by the hour.

    Synthesis: deployment is chosen per workload, not per company, and “hybrid” is the name for having chosen twice on purpose. The trap runs the other way too — reaching for community whenever a stem mentions more than one organization, when what community actually requires is one rulebook they all live under.

    One honest closing note, because Objective 1 asks you to weigh both sides. Passing the five-trait test is not a virtue certificate. The same traits that make cloud attractive are the ones that generate its four standing risks: broad network access makes you useless without connectivity, pooling and platform depth make you costly to leave, somebody else’s data centre raises compliance questions, and measured service means an unwatched bill can run away from you. Every one of those has a standard design answer — offline-first sync, an exit plan, encryption and residency controls, budgets and alerts. Architects do not deny the risks; they design around them, and that is what the capstone will ask you to do for Harbor Lane Books.

    10 of 10 terms
    S1
    You provision the resource yourself, in minutes, with no purchase order and no technician. Ordering a physical server takes weeks.
    S1
    Reachable over standard networks from phones, laptops and other servers. One wired terminal in one building is not cloud.
    S1 · S7
    One pool of provider hardware serves many consumers at once, isolated by virtualization. Pooling is why prices are low.
    S1 · S11
    Capacity stretches and shrinks with demand, often automatically, so that to the customer it appears unlimited.
    S1 · S11
    Usage is metered like electricity — per hour, per gigabyte, per request — and reported back to you. Wonderful, until an unmonitored bill surprises you.
    S1 · S8
    The condition of many customers sharing one pooled infrastructure. You cannot ask a public provider to ban your co-tenants; that is how public clouds work at all.
    S1
    Shared infrastructure rented to anyone with a credit card — maximum pooling, minimum cost, fastest start. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
    S1 · S8
    Cloud-style infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, on premises or hosted, trading cost for control. It still has to clear all five gates.
    S1
    Infrastructure shared by organizations with a common need and a common regulatory regime — five hospitals on one HIPAA platform.
    S1 · S8 · S12
    A deliberate combination: sensitive systems stay private while spiky or everyday workloads burst to public. Most real enterprises end up here.
    Next The abstraction ladder
    Objectives 2, 3 and 4 · Sessions 1, 2 and 3

    IVThe abstraction ladder

    IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are not three definitions. They are one line, drawn across one stack, in three different places.

    Every system in this course is the same nine layers in the same order: data and access, applications, runtime, middleware, operating system, virtualization, servers, storage, networking. Nothing about a service model changes that stack. Each model draws one horizontal line across it and hands everything below the line to somebody else — and the only thing that separates the three is how high the line is drawn.

    In the margin

    When you flip a light switch you neither know nor care which power plant made the electricity. Save a photo “to the cloud” and you do not know which disk in which building holds it — and that is the point, not an oversight.

    See Plate 04 for the ladder that line climbs.

    Start at the bottom rung, which is not a cloud model at all. On-premises means you operate all nine layers and buy the hardware they run on. IaaS hands the bottom four to a provider — virtualization, servers, storage, networking — so you rent the computer and still install, patch and secure everything from the operating system up. PaaS keeps only your code and your data on your side of the line: there is no server you can log into, because the server is not your problem. SaaS puts the line above the whole stack; you bring a browser, your users and your data.

    The course’s rule of thumb is worth saying out loud until it is automatic: IaaS = rent the computer. PaaS = rent the platform. SaaS = rent the finished software. Deshawn’s four developers at Kettle & Crumb do not know which machine runs their ordering app and have no way to find out — they know that git push makes the new version live. Marisol’s team at Pelican Point Outfitters knows exactly which two virtual machines it runs, which is why an unpatched Linux kernel on the guest operating system was hers to answer for and not the provider’s.

    Exam trap

    A product does not carry one permanent label. The chatbot your aunt uses is SaaS; the same model behind an API key is PaaS to the developer calling it; the GPU fleet that trained it is IaaS at maximum scale. The exam never asks what a product is. It asks which layer you are renting.

    Climbing the ladder removes work and removes control in the same motion, and you cannot buy one without paying the other. IaaS is the most flexible model because you can run almost anything on it — and “flexible” is a synonym for “your job.” SaaS is the fastest to stand up — 240 mailboxes created in an afternoon instead of installed on 240 machines — and it will never let you change core workflow code, because that code ships to every customer or to none.

    The line also has a floor it can never rise above. Accounts and identity, MFA and single sign-on policy, retention and sharing rules, data classification, seat deprovisioning, and the exit plan stay with the buyer at every rung. Three weeks after Harbor Lane Books let a store manager go, she was still reading company mail from home: the vendor ran every layer flawlessly and the failure was entirely Harbor Lane’s. “SaaS customers manage nothing” is not a simplification, it is the misconception the exam is built to catch.

    Say the sentence, not the count

    The course ships two stack painters and they differ by one row on PaaS — one marks only Data & access yours, the other marks Data & access plus Applications. Do not memorise a number. Say “under PaaS I keep my code and my data,” which is right under either painter and is the definition itself.

    Where the line belongs is not a matter of taste, and it is not decided by the technology. It is decided by two sentences in the brief: the deepest layer somebody has promised the client can still change, and the number of layers the people you actually employ can operate on a Tuesday. Set both at the bench, predict which one binds, and then read the instrument.

    Item 04.1Objectives 2–4Discrimination

    In the GitHub Pages lab you edit index.html in GitHub’s browser editor, commit to main, and a minute later the live URL serves your change. A classmate asks which service models that one minute touched.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The ladder inverted. You deploy your own content to Pages and merely use the editor, so the two labels are the wrong way round. Nothing here is on-premises either: GitHub owns the building, not you.

    • Correct

      Three rungs in one minute. The editor is finished software you use in a browser; Pages takes your content and builds, deploys, hosts and serves it; the fleet beneath is GitHub’s own infrastructure.

    • No

      Delivery channel mistaken for service model. A browser is how SaaS reaches you, not proof that everything reached through one is SaaS. Pages still runs code you supplied.

    • No

      Hardware ownership mistaken for what is rented. Somebody always owns the metal; by this logic every cloud service on earth would be IaaS and the word would carry no information.

    Synthesis: the label is not a property of the product, it is a property of the layer you happen to be renting at that moment. That is why one company’s platform can be three service models before lunch, and why the useful question is never “what is this” but “where is the line for me.”

    Item 04.2Objectives 2–4Named trap

    A vendor’s slide reads: “We are not IaaS, PaaS or SaaS — we are DBaaS, the fourth service model.” The product is a managed database: you design tables, connect over a URL, and there is no host you can log into. How do you classify it?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      XaaS mistaken for a fourth rung. Every “anything as a service” still resolves to IaaS, PaaS or SaaS depending on how much of the stack it takes off you. The ladder has three rungs and a floor; marketing cannot add one.

    • No

      The stack read from its bottom layer. Somebody always owns servers. What is rented here is a running database service, not the machine it happens to sit on.

    • Correct

      Read by who the customer is. The customer is a developer’s application; the provider runs the OS, the engine, patching and backups; and the PaaS test holds exactly — there is no server you can log into.

    • No

      The four-part SaaS test half-applied. Network delivery and a subscription satisfy two criteria. A managed database is not a finished application an end user does work in, so it fails the first and most important one.

    Synthesis: XaaS is a sales taxonomy and the ladder is an engineering one. Translate every “-aaS” into the same question — how many of the nine layers stop being ours? — and the fourth-model claim evaporates while the useful part of the pitch survives.

    The industry now sells nearly every IT function this way, which is where the sprawl of “-aaS” names comes from. Six are named in this course, and each is a forward pointer as much as a category: identity returns in Session 4 and again in the capstone, storage in Session 5, and disaster recovery in Session 9, where recovery objectives decide which tier you can afford. None of them is a new rung.

    The six XaaS categories the course names — and what each one actually rents
    CategoryWhat you actually rentNamed on the page
    IDaaSLogin itself — single sign-on, multi-factor, the directory of who existsOkta, Microsoft Entra ID
    STaaSCapacity by the gigabyte-month, with multiple copies kept for youAmazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Dropbox
    DBaaSA database you design tables in and never SSH intoAmazon RDS, MongoDB Atlas
    DRaaSContinuous replication and a failover to call when the building floodsNo product named — Session 9 prices the tier instead
    FaaSOne function, billed per invocation, with no server anywhere in viewAWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers
    AIaaSIntelligence by the tokenChatbots, model APIs, and the GPU fleets beneath both

    The clearest way to feel the rung you are standing on is to notice what the shell prompt looks like. At one rung you have one; at the next there is nothing to log into; at the last there is no deploy step at all, only settings — and the settings never stop being yours.

    # IaaS — the provider hands you a shell, so everything you install is yours
ssh admin@pelican-web-01 && sudo apt install nginx   # and yours to patch, forever

# PaaS — there is no shell; the platform builds, deploys and scales
git push paas main                                   # 47 objects; web.1 up in 3.1s

# SaaS — there is no deploy step at all, only settings
#   which are still your job: MFA, retention, and who keeps a mailbox on Friday

    Item 04.3Objectives 2–3Application

    Grimaldi & Voss will not give up its 14-step conflict-check process, and the SaaS intake screens cannot be configured into that shape. The firm has no infrastructure staff and no appetite to hire any. Where should the line sit for that one workflow?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      Rented as high as the requirement allows. The differentiator is the fourteen steps, so keep Applications and Data and rent the seven layers under them. Build, deploy and scale belong to the platform, and nobody has to be hired to run an operating system.

    • No

      Configuration confused with a private fork. SaaS core workflow code ships to every customer or to none. There is no private fork at any price — only custom fields, templates and toggles.

    • No

      Control bought well past the point of need. IaaS would run the workflow and would also hand the firm five layers of chores — patching, deploy scripts, scaling — that it has just said it will not staff.

    • No

      Bespoke software mistaken for bespoke hardware. Nothing about a fourteen-step process requires owning metal. It requires owning the code that encodes the steps, which is one layer, not nine.

    Synthesis: rent up to the highest rung that still lets you change what you must change. Here the must-change layer is Applications, so the line sits directly beneath it — one rung higher and the requirement is unbuildable, one rung lower and the chores are unstaffable. That single sentence answers every service-model scenario on the exam.

    8 of 8 terms
    S1
    A simple interface that hides the real machinery underneath. You trade control of hardware for freedom from hardware.
    S1 · S3
    Rent the computer. The provider owns data centres, hardware and the virtualization layer; you operate the guest OS and everything above it. Amazon EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine.
    S2
    Rent the platform. The provider runs the OS, runtime, web server, middleware, databases and networking; you supply the application code and its data. There is no server you can log into.
    S2
    Rent the finished software — a complete application over the internet, billed by subscription, with the vendor running every layer. You bring a browser, your users and your data.
    S1
    You operate all nine layers and buy the hardware. The baseline the other three rungs are measured against, not a fourth cloud model.
    S1
    The pattern of selling nearly every IT function as a metered service — IDaaS, STaaS, DBaaS, DRaaS, FaaS, AIaaS. Never a fourth service model; each still resolves to one of the three.
    S1 · S3
    The software that slices one physical machine into isolated virtual ones. Under IaaS it is the provider’s, and the guest OS directly above it is yours — that is where the line is drawn.
    S2
    Custom fields, templates and toggles — the only kind of change SaaS offers. Core workflow code ships to all customers or none, and private forks do not exist.
    Decision rule

    Rent up to the highest rung that still lets you change what you must change. One rung higher and the requirement is unbuildable; one rung lower and the chores are unstaffable.

    Next The responsibility line
    Objective 7 · Sessions 2, 3 and 8

    VThe responsibility line

    Eight duties, three columns, one staircase — the discriminator this exam reuses more than any other.

    Every cloud contract is really two contracts stapled together: the provider secures the cloud itself, and you secure what you put in it. Between those two halves sits a middle that slides — and the entire skill this module builds is knowing exactly where it stops for the product you just bought.

    In the margin

    IaaS hands you a virtual machine the way a landlord hands you an apartment. The roof, the wiring and the lock on the street door are theirs. Everything you carry inside is yours — including the smoke alarm nobody tests.

    See Plate 5 for the staircase that line climbs.

    Write the eight duties down the side of a page and the three service models across the top, and something useful happens: five of the eight rows never move. Physical data-centre security, hardware and disk disposal, and the hypervisor are the provider’s in every column, at every price. Identity, access and MFA, and data classification and sharing configuration, are yours in every column, at every price. Only three rows in the middle — application code, runtime and middleware, and guest-OS patching — change hands, and they change hands in discrete steps, not by degrees.

    That is why Gartner’s much-quoted prediction — that through 2025, 99% of cloud security failures would be the customer’s fault rather than the provider’s — is not a slur on customers. It is arithmetic. The provider’s rows are patched fleet-wide within hours by people whose only job is patching. Your rows are patched by whoever is left after the sysadmin resigns in March.

    Exam trap

    “We moved to the cloud, so security is handled.” No sentence has preceded more breaches. Migration moves at most three rows; it never moves the two at the top, which is precisely where the failures live.

    The reverse error costs just as much. Marisol’s team at Pelican Point Outfitters ran two virtual machines on IaaS for four months and never touched the guest operating system, on the reasonable-sounding theory that the provider was doing it. Attackers used a Linux kernel hole that had been patched upstream nine weeks earlier. The provider’s incident report was short: hypervisor current, hosts current, network current. Everything the provider owned was clean. The one row Pelican Point owned was not.

    The plate answers a question of ownership. The bench below answers the question a manager actually asks at 2 a.m., which is narrower and harsher: who is holding the pager? Ownership and paging are the same thing here, and the only two facts you need are the column you bought and the row the incident landed on.

    Item 5.1Objective 7Discrimination

    Mangrove Books runs its storefront on a PaaS platform. On Tuesday morning a critical operating-system vulnerability is announced. The owner wants to know who patches the OS beneath the store.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The IaaS duty imported into PaaS. Administering the guest OS “exactly as if the VM sat in your closet” is the IaaS row. Moving up to PaaS is the precise step that hands that row back — if Mangrove still had to schedule OS windows, it did not buy a platform.

    • No

      The layer denied. Every platform runs on an operating system; you simply never touch it. A layer you cannot see is not a layer that is absent, and “nobody patches it” is never an answer this matrix produces.

    • No

      Identity vouching mistaken for infrastructure operation. A certificate authority vouches for a domain’s identity during the TLS handshake. It operates no servers, patches no kernels, and appears nowhere in the eight rows.

    • Correct

      Two rows changed hands. Guest-OS patching and runtime & middleware are exactly the two rows that flip from you to the provider on the IaaS→PaaS step. Application code, identity, and data classification stay with Mangrove.

    Synthesis: the layer alone never answers the question. “Who patches the OS?” has three different correct answers — you, the provider, the provider — depending on which column you are standing in. Name the layer, name the model, then read the cell; skipping the middle step is what makes this the most-missed item on the exam.

    Exam trap

    “The IaaS provider patches the guest OS as part of the monthly fee.” That describes managed services and PaaS, not IaaS. The tell is simple: if the provider patched your guest OS, you would not have root on it.

    Item 5.2Objective 2Misconception

    Harbor Lane Books retires its closet Exchange server for SaaS email at $6 per user per month for 240 staff. The office manager tells the board that the company now manages nothing. What correction do you make?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The deployment model smuggled in. Public versus private is a deployment question about who else shares the pool. The customer’s top two rows are set by the service model and stay hers in either — a private tenancy buys isolation, not absolution.

    • Correct

      Only the top two rows survive the trip. Identity and access, and data classification and sharing, never leave the customer at any service model. That is why disabling a departed employee’s account on day one is Harbor Lane’s job and no vendor’s.

    • No

      “Nothing at all” — the classic double failure. It fails twice: the bottom rows were never hers to hand over, and the top two were never the vendor’s to take. Accounts, retention policy and data governance do not outsource.

    • No

      A guest OS invented under a finished application. SaaS customers administer no operating system at all. The row exists — every platform runs on one — but it sits three rows below where Harbor Lane’s side of the line ends.

    Synthesis: SaaS does not mean “the vendor does everything.” It means the sliding middle has finished sliding, and what is left is a thin stripe of two rows — identity and data — that is exactly where Gartner put 99% of cloud security failures. The narrower your side of the matrix gets, the more concentrated your remaining risk becomes.

    The line also decides what a command can even reach. The same duty — keep the operating system current — is a shell command at IaaS and an unreachable layer at SaaS, while the two rows that stay yours look identical in both:

    # IaaS — row 5 is yours, and it is reachable, which is the whole point
ssh ops@pelican-web-01 'sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get -y upgrade'

# SaaS — the same duty exists, but there is no host to log into.
# What is still yours is never a shell command; it is a setting:
sharing:   internal-only     # row 1 · data classification  → yours
mfa:       required-for-all  # row 2 · identity and access  → yours
offboard:  same-day          # row 2 again — the one that gets skipped

    Item 5.3Objective 7Structure

    Petal & Stem Florists holds three quotes for the same workload — IaaS, PaaS and SaaS — and asks, in one sentence, what actually changes about its security obligations across the three. Which answer is structurally correct?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The gradual-slide picture. Nothing here is gradual. Five of the eight rows are fixed at every model, and the three that move do so in discrete steps — two at the IaaS→PaaS boundary, one at PaaS→SaaS. A duty is never half-owned.

    • No

      The line drawn too low. Facility security and disk disposal belonged to the provider from the first invoice, so they cannot transfer. Drawing the line beneath them makes Petal & Stem the owner of a hypervisor it has never seen.

    • Correct

      Three slide, five are nailed down. Application code, runtime & middleware, and guest-OS patching are the only rows that change hands across the whole trip. The top two never leave Petal & Stem; the bottom three never leave the provider.

    • No

      The invoice mistaken for the contract. The service model is a security boundary before it is a price. Two quotes at the same monthly figure can hand Petal & Stem five rows or two — and the cheaper column is often the one with more work in it.

    Synthesis: count before you argue — eight rows, three movable, five fixed. Every “who is responsible?” question resolves to locating one row and one column, and five of the eight rows do not need the column at all. That is why the fastest way to answer these items is to check the row first: if it is data, identity, hypervisor, hardware or facility, the service model is a distraction.

    5 of 5 terms
    S8
    The contractual split of security duties: the provider secures the cloud itself, the customer secures what they put in it, and the middle slides with the service model. Eight rows, three of them movable.
    S3
    The OS running inside your virtual machine — the first thing on the customer’s side of the line at IaaS, and the last thing to leave it on the way up the ladder.
    S8
    Application code, runtime & middleware, and guest-OS patching: the only three duties that change owner between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Everything else is fixed in both directions.
    S2
    Removing accounts and paid seats when people leave or licences go unused. A customer duty at every service model — never the provider’s, and never automatic.
    S8
    Destroying the encryption keys so every copy, replica and backup becomes permanent noise — the customer’s only real lever over disks it will never touch. An exit strategy chosen at entry.
    Decision rule

    Name the row first. If it is data, identity, hypervisor, hardware or facility, the service model is irrelevant and you already have the answer. Only then does the column matter.

    Next What the line costs
    Objectives 1 and 2 · Sessions 1, 2 and 3

    VIRent, own, and the crossing

    Every architecture you will draw after this page has a price. Two lines, one crossing, and the four cost lines the model never carried.

    A client asks two money questions, and they are not the same question. The first is how much, and it is answered with arithmetic. The second is what shape — committed up front against a guess, or metered monthly and stoppable — and it is answered with a decision about risk. The cloud changes the second answer far more reliably than it changes the first.

    In the margin

    A board never asks for “CapEx to OpEx.” It says “I am not signing another cheque for hardware we outgrow in a year” and “I need to be able to stop paying for this.” Those two sentences are the whole of the shift.

    See Plate 6 for the month the two lines cross.

    Devon, the CFO in the Session 1 scenario, is holding two quotes: $180,000 of servers replaced every four years, or roughly $4,200 a month of rented capacity. The course does the sum against its own sales pitch. Forty-eight months of rent is $201,600 — $21,600 more than buying the hardware outright. The honest sentence is the one Devon actually gives the board: buying commits capital up front, and cloud converts it to an operating expense that scales with use and can stop at any time.

    Notice what the extra $21,600 buys. The $180,000 is committed on day one against a guess about year-four demand, and the guess is made by the people least able to see year four. Renting buys out of that guess: no sizing risk, no refresh cycle to finance, no utilisation problem — and “most owned servers idle” is the industry's own confession. Steady, predictable, fully utilised workloads can still favour owning. That is a real answer, not a concession.

    Exam trap

    “Cloud is always cheaper.” The course hands you the arithmetic that disproves it: $4,200 × 48 = $201,600 against $180,000 of hardware. Cloud wins on flexibility and avoided risk — not automatically on totals.

    Item 6.1Objective 1Arithmetic

    Devon is choosing between $180,000 of servers replaced every four years and roughly $4,200 a month of rented capacity. The board asks what the financial difference is, beyond the totals. Which answer survives the arithmetic?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Slogan mistaken for arithmetic. $4,200 × 48 = $201,600 against $180,000 of hardware. The course runs this sum against its own sales pitch precisely so that you never say “always” in front of a CFO.

    • No

      The asset argument, left unpriced. Servers depreciate, need refreshing at year four, and were sized against a guess about year-four demand. Owning wins when a workload is steady, predictable and fully utilised — not by default.

    • Correct

      Both columns read, and the gap named. Renting costs $21,600 more here, and the difference is the shape of the payment: capital committed up front against an operating expense that scales with use and can stop.

    • No

      Staff costs assumed to vanish. Someone still configures, secures and monitors cloud systems. The provider absorbs patching, hardware failure and physical security; architecture and operations stay on your payroll.

    Synthesis: the board asked about shape, not size. CapEx buys an asset and a commitment; OpEx buys optionality and a meter. Say the total, say the gap, then say what the gap buys — a CFO will accept “more expensive and worth it” far sooner than a number that turns out to be wrong.

    The same crossing happens along a second axis, and this is the one the exam prefers, because it is about scale rather than time. Session 2 fixes the horizon at 36 months and compares two columns. Renting is seats × rate × 36. Owning is (seats × licence × 1.6) + hardware, where the ×1.6 is not a fudge factor: it is the perpetual licence plus a support contract charged at 20% of licence cost every year for three years.

    Exam trap

    “The two totals are within $1,000 — call it a tie.” That answer only appears when the support contract and the hardware are left out. They are the two lines buyers omit, and both belong to the owning column.

    The 36-month model line by line — and the line each column loses first
    LineColumnIn the modelCourse value
    SubscriptionRentedseats × rate × 36$792 a seat at $22
    Perpetual licenceOwnedseats × licence$400 a seat
    Support contractOwned20% of licence a year, three years×1.6 on the licence
    Hardware and setupOwnedone fixed sum$12,000
    Admin labour, refresh, outageOwnednot modelledpriced by hand
    Migration effort, unused seatsRentednot modelledpriced by hand

    Write both columns out and a third number falls out of them for free. Renting costs a fixed amount per seat over three years and so does owning; the difference between those two per-seat figures is what the fixed hardware cost has to be spread across. Divide one by the other and you have the crossover point — the seat count at which owning stops costing more. At $22 a seat a month against a $400 licence, that is $12,000 ÷ ($792 − $640) ≈ 79 seats. The course calls it the single most useful number in any rent-versus-buy argument, because it converts a quarrel about philosophy into a question about size.

gap   =  95040 - 88800               #   $6,240   inside 10% of $95,040 -> a cost TIE
cross =  12000 / (22*36 - 400*1.6)   #      78.9 -> 79 seats: fixed cost / per-seat gap

    Set the three dials, say out loud which column you think is cheaper and roughly where the two lines cross, then commit.

    Item 6.2Objective 2Computation

    A 120-seat firm compares SaaS at $14 per seat per month against a $400-per-seat perpetual licence plus $12,000 of server hardware, on the course's 36-month model. Which pair of totals is right?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The support contract dropped. 120 × $400 + $12,000 is $60,000 only if the licence is bought once and never supported. The model charges 20% of licence a year for three years — that is the ×1.6.

    • Correct

      Every line of both columns counted. 120 × $14 × 36 = $60,480, and 120 × $400 × 1.6 + $12,000 = $88,800. The $28,320 gap sits well outside the 10% tie band, so it is a real difference.

    • No

      The gap reported as a total. $28,320 is the distance between the two columns, not the cost of owning. This is the slide-deck error a CFO catches in the first minute of the meeting.

    • No

      Hardware exiled to another budget. Capital spending is still spending. Moving $12,000 to a different page of the deck does not remove it from the three years being compared.

    Synthesis: the two lines buyers omit are the support contract and the hardware, and both omissions move the answer the same way — toward owning. Write the model out in full, seats × rate × 36 against (seats × licence × 1.6) + hardware, and the argument becomes arithmetic anybody in the room can check.

    The meter is what makes the rented column honest, and it is also what makes it dangerous. Measured service bills per hour, per gigabyte, per request, so waste shows up as a number rather than as an idle rack nobody looks at — which is how Opal Threads discovered six forgotten test VMs in May, $4,100 into a nine-week bill, at 2% CPU. The same trait cuts the other way: unused seats are metered too. Twelve paid seats nobody uses is 12 × $8 × 36 = $3,456 of pure waste, and it is the fastest-fixable line on any SaaS invoice.

    Decision rule

    Check the sign of the per-seat gap before you divide. If renting costs less per seat than owning, there is no crossing at all and no seat count will rescue the purchase. Only when renting costs more per seat does a crossing exist — at fixed cost ÷ per-seat gap.

    Item 6.3Objectives 1 and 2Discrimination

    At $22 a seat a month, a $400 licence and $12,000 of hardware, the crossing sits at 79 seats. Harbor Lane Books has 240 employees, and the owner concludes the arithmetic has settled it: buy the servers. What is the strongest professional response?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The crossing promoted to a verdict. It is a starting point, not a finding. It tells you which side of the argument scale has put you on, and nothing whatever about the lines the model never carried.

    • No

      A moving number mistaken for a broken one. A discount moves the crossing; it does not abolish it. Re-run the division at the quoted rate — that is a two-minute job, not grounds for abandoning the model.

    • No

      An equal cost used as a tie-breaker. The AI feature is a metered API bill that lands on both columns identically, so it moves both totals by the same amount and can never change which one wins.

    • Correct

      The omitted lines named before the signature. Patching, backups and 2 a.m. restarts are unpriced on the owning side; migration effort and seats nobody deprovisions are unpriced on the renting side. Price them and 240 seats can still come out renting.

    Synthesis: the crossover converts an argument about philosophy into an argument about scale, and that is the whole of its value — it does not end the conversation. Quote the crossing, then say out loud which unpriced line you would have to be wrong about for the verdict to flip. That sentence is what separates a consultant from a calculator.

    Two more numbers belong in the same argument, and both are timing rather than size. Reserved instances trade a one-to-three-year commitment for a 30–60% discount — Meridian Media's three-year rate is 55% below on-demand — but signing on day one of a migration buys that discount against a footprint roughly 1.4× the one you will end up running, which the simulator prices at $1,680 a month, about $20,160 across a twelve-month lock. And at the other end of the scale, Ostara Labs' 512-GPU cluster is used about six weeks a year: roughly 88% idle, $15M to buy. Renting is not a philosophy. It is what you do with an asset you cannot keep busy.

    8 of 8 terms
    S1
    A large purchase of assets, committed up front and depreciating from the day it arrives. Devon's $180,000 of servers, replaced every four years.
    S1
    Ongoing spend that scales with actual use and can be stopped at any time. Roughly $4,200 a month of rented capacity.
    S1 · S11
    Usage metered like electricity — per hour, per gigabyte, per request. It is what makes OpEx honest, and “wonderful, until an unmonitored bill surprises you.”
    S2
    20% of total licence cost every year. Over three years it turns the licence line into ×1.6 — the single most-omitted line in a rent-versus-buy comparison.
    S2
    The seat count at which the fixed cost has spread thin enough for owning to stop costing more. Fixed cost ÷ per-seat gap; ≈79 seats at $22 a seat against a $400 licence.
    S2
    Money spent on paid seats nobody uses — 12 seats × $8 × 36 months is $3,456. The fastest-fixable line in a SaaS bill.
    S3
    Matching provisioned capacity to measured demand. 32 vCPU and 128 GB down to 4 vCPU and 16 GB saved $1,008 a month — about $12,096 a year.
    S12
    A one-to-three-year capacity commitment bought for a 30–60% discount. A 55% discount on the wrong servers is a 45% overpayment with a contract attached.
    Next Growing and shrinking on demand
    Objectives 1 and 4 · Sessions 1, 3 and 11

    VIICapacity that moves

    Three answers to one spike, and the single threshold that prices whichever one you pick.

    Three words do the work in this module, and points are lost by treating them as synonyms. Scaling up buys a bigger machine. Scaling out buys more machines and a door to route between them. Elasticity buys neither: it buys a rule that changes the number of machines by itself, in both directions, on a meter that bills by the hour.

    In the margin

    Two verbs and a rule. Scale up (verb), scale out (verb), elasticity — the rule that keeps performing the verb while you sleep, and performs it backwards at midnight.

    Plate 7 A draws all three against one day of demand.

    The course’s pizza shop is worth keeping. Scale up is one giant oven. Scale out is more ordinary ovens plus a person routing orders to them. Elasticity is ovens that appear at the dinner rush and vanish at midnight, charged by the oven-hour. Everything that matters is in the third sentence: direction is a decision you make once, elasticity is a rule that keeps making it, and the meter is what turns the rule into money.

    Scaling up is simple and it ends. In the TicketBlitz catalogue a single machine comes in four sizes — M holds 1,000 requests a minute for $90, L holds 2,000 for $180, XL holds 4,000 for $400, XXL holds 8,000 for $900 — and above 8,000 there is nothing left to buy. Push the simulator to 8,250 requests a minute and its verdict simply reads UP impossible. Before that ceiling, up also carries two quieter costs: the resize is a restart, and what you have at the end is one bigger single point of failure.

    Exam trap

    Calling automatic scaling “scale out.” Scale-out is a direction; elasticity is the automatic, bidirectional, metered behaviour. An option that says a shop “scaled out” when its fleet grew for six hours and shrank by itself before midnight has named the direction and missed the trait being tested.

    Scaling out needs a front door, and the load balancer is it. It receives every request and hands it to one of a pool of servers — round-robin takes turns, least-connections feeds the least busy machine — while users see a single address. It earns its $18 a month twice. Once for scale, because it is what makes a second server useful at all. Once for fault tolerance, because it probes every server continuously (an HTTP request to /healthz every few seconds) and pulls a failing one out of rotation without being asked — which is more than DNS will ever do for you, since DNS points at the balancer and neither detects a dead backend nor routes around one. BrightCart’s server #3 hung on a Tuesday at 2 PM and stayed effectively dead for six hours: zero support tickets, normal revenue, and the other three quietly absorbing its quarter of the traffic, each rising from about 25% of the load to about 33%.

    Exam trap

    “A load balancer adds capacity.” It spreads load across capacity you are already paying for. Balance three drowning servers and you have three evenly drowning servers.

    Money separates the first two answers earlier than most people expect. In the Session 1 model a small server takes 500 requests a minute and costs $40, and the balancer adds a flat $18 — so the scale-out bill is ceil(traffic ÷ 500) × $40 + $18, which is worth memorising because Lab A grades it. At 3,000 requests a minute that is six servers: 6 × $40 + $18 = $258. Run the same traffic through the scale-up catalogue and one machine is cheaper at only two points on the whole slider.

    The TicketBlitz catalogue: where scale-up stops being cheaper, and where it stops being possible
    Traffic, req/minScale out · ceil(t ÷ 500) × $40 + $18Scale up · first tier that fitsCheaper
    5001 server · $58M · $90out
    7502 servers · $98M · $90up
    1,0002 servers · $98M · $90up
    1,2503 servers · $138L · $180out
    2,0004 servers · $178L · $180out
    4,0008 servers · $338XL · $400out
    8,00016 servers · $658XXL · $900out
    8,25017 servers · $698no tier existsout only
    Decision rule

    Below the crossover, prefer one machine: it is simpler and cheaper. Above it, scale out wins on price and survives one server dying. Past the biggest box in the catalogue there is no decision left to make.

    Session 3 then changes the rate card, and reading which model a question is in is itself an exam skill. In the load-balancer simulator a server is rated for 1,000 requests a minute and costs $48; it is green to 700, amber from 701 to 950, saturated from 951 to 1,050, and above 1,050 it starts refusing work. The 700 is not decoration. It is the 70% line an autoscaling policy aims to hold, and it is the number the survivors of a failure must still be under. That is where N+1 comes from: at 2,400 requests a minute, 2,400 ÷ 700 = 3.43, so four survivors are needed, so you run five. Each of the five carries 480; lose one and the four remaining carry 600 — still green, and no customer notices. The same spare capacity is what makes a zero-downtime deploy possible: drain one server, upgrade it, return it, repeat.

    Item 7.1Objective 4Computation

    Meridian Market forecasts 4,900 requests a minute for Friday’s flash sale. Each web server is rated for 1,000 and stays green to 700, and the runbook requires the fleet to stay green with one server dead. How many servers, and what is the month at $48 a server plus an $18 balancer?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Rated capacity read as usable capacity. 1,000 is where a server saturates, not where it is comfortable. Five servers put every machine at 980 a minute — inside the saturated band before the sale even opens, with nothing left for a failure.

    • Correct

      Sized on the green number, then plus one. 4,900 ÷ 700 = 7 exactly, so seven is the peak fleet and the eighth is the spare. Eight servers carry 612 each; lose one and the seven survivors carry 700 — exactly on the line. 8 × $48 + $18 = $402.

    • No

      The +1 forgotten, and the balancer credited with capacity. Seven is the peak fleet, not the survivable one. Lose a server and six carry 817 a minute each — deep in amber — because the balancer distributes an overload evenly, it does not absorb it.

    • No

      N+1 confused with 2N. Doubling is what you buy to survive losing a whole availability zone. Here it doubles the bill to insure against a failure mode the runbook never named, and the exam rewards the sentence you were actually given.

    Synthesis: N+1 is one sentence of arithmetic — divide the forecast by the green number, round up, add one. The 700 does two jobs at once: it is where the autoscaler should already be adding a server, and it is the ceiling the survivors of a failure must still sit under. Sizing for the peak and stopping is the single most common way to pass the maths and fail the sale.

    Everything so far has been a fixed count. Elasticity replaces the count with a rule, and the rule has exactly one number that matters: the trigger — the per-server load at which the group adds an instance. Set it high and you run lean and have almost no runway when demand jumps. Set it low and you always have standing capacity, and you pay for it at four in the morning. Plate 7 B is that arithmetic on one ruler.

    Bench 07 puts that question against a real day. Harbor Lane samples its Saturday in eight three-hour blocks — 400, 500, 1,400, 2,600, 3,000, 4,200, 9,000 and 1,800 requests a minute — and the group sizes itself as max(2, ceil(demand ÷ trigger)) + spare. When demand steps up, new instances need five minutes to answer, and for those five minutes the fleet is still the one the previous block sized: anything above 1,050 a minute per standing server is refused. The month is the average fleet at $48 a server plus $18 for the balancer. Predict the two numbers out loud before you commit — that is the point of the instrument.
