    Set the trigger and the spare, say out loud how many requests the day will drop and what the month will cost, then commit.

    The instrument is blunt about the trade in both directions. At the course’s own 70% line the day costs $240 and refuses 16,000 requests — 2,500 at the morning ramp and 13,500 in the five minutes after the doors open. Drop the trigger to 500 and the group is already standing at nine servers at 18:00, which covers the step, and the same day costs $318 with nothing lost. The difference is $78 a month of capacity the demand never touched. That is the entire argument, priced: $78 buys 16,000 orders.

    There is a third dial the bench deliberately does not give you, and it is the one a professional reaches for first. The on-sale is on the calendar. A scheduled action can raise the floor at 17:45 and drop it again at 23:00, which costs nothing at all on the other 23 hours and removes the warm-up problem entirely. Elasticity has to react; a schedule does not.

    # Harbor Lane · web tier autoscaling group
min: 2                     # the floor you park at overnight — never the peak
max: 20                    # the ceiling that stops a bad day becoming a bad month
target_per_instance: 500   # the trigger, in requests/min. NOT the rated 1,000
warmup: 300s               # 5 min of boot; the runway 1,050 - 500 has to cover it
scale_in_cooldown: 900s    # shrink slowly: flapping costs more than one idle server
scheduled:
  - at: "17:45 Sat"        # the on-sale is on the calendar, so pre-scale for it
    min: 14                # elasticity reacts; a scheduled action does not have to
    Decision rule

    If the spike is on the calendar, schedule the capacity. If it is not, buy runway with a lower trigger. Either way, never park the peak fleet for 24 hours to cover an event that lasts three.

    Item 7.2Objective 1Discrimination

    NoodleNow is named on a national broadcast and goes from 1,000 to 10,000 requests a minute for three hours. An adviser proposes grid computing — “split the work across many machines.” What is wrong with the proposal?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The words “many machines” mistaken for the technique. Grid and elasticity both end with many machines running, which is exactly why the exam pairs them. Grid is defined by what it does to the work — it cuts one job into pieces — not by the size of the resulting fleet.

    • No

      Right formula, wrong question. The 2% per node is real: it is why 64 nodes return only about 44% efficiency on the 3,200 core-hour job. But overhead is what makes a grid inefficient, not what makes it the wrong tool for web traffic.

    • No

      The money question substituted for the shape question. Renting for the burst is correct advice about a grid, and irrelevant here: no amount of rental changes the fact that there is no single large computation to divide.

    • Correct

      Matched on the shape of the work. Ten thousand small, independent requests a minute are cloned-server work: identical stateless copies behind a balancer, with the count rising and falling automatically. That is elasticity, and it is the mirror image of grid.

    Synthesis: match the technique to the shape of the work, not to the word “many.” One enormous computation splits across nodes and pays coordination for the privilege — doubling the machines never halves the time. Millions of independent requests clone the server and let the balancer spread them. The lineage is real, though: grid’s “many cheap machines beat one giant machine” became scale-out, and it is the same idea now wired together as a GPU training cluster.

    Exam trap

    Scaling out a write master. A single PostgreSQL primary cannot simply be photocopied — a second write master is how the same seat gets sold twice. Write paths scale out through sharding or read replicas, which is a re-architecture project, not a button. And scaling out a memory leak just gives you more nodes marching toward out-of-memory, with a bigger bill.

    Item 7.3Objective 8Operations

    At 02:10 TicketNest’s checkout latency doubles. The web tier’s CPU is flat at 41% and its autoscaling group has not moved; the single PostgreSQL write master is pinned at 96% with a lengthening lock queue. Which lever?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      The lever matched to the state of the tier. The metric that moved first names the tier, and this one is stateful. Writes cannot be cloned, so up is the only direction available — and because the resize is a restart, it is announced rather than improvised while you relieve the master with caching and read replicas.

    • No

      The emergency lever aimed at the wrong tier. Scale-out is right for stateless copies and the web tier’s flat 41% says the web tier is not the constraint. Every extra copy opens more connections to the one master that is already saturated.

    • No

      The memory-leak fingerprint applied to a lock queue. A restart answers a staircase that resets on restart and tracks a deploy. Here it takes the only write path offline and hands you back the same saturated master a minute later.

    • No

      Failover for a fault that has not happened. Failover answers “unreachable,” not “saturated.” Nothing here is unreachable, so you would relocate the identical overload onto a cold cache and a farther replica, and pay for the move.

    Synthesis: read which metric moved first, then ask whether that tier is stateless. Stateless and hot → out, and the autoscaling group can do it while you sleep. Stateful and hot → up, in a window. Unreachable → failover. A staircase that resets on restart → rolling restart, then roll the deploy back. One lever, chosen by the fingerprint — and every other lever on this dashboard actively makes the incident worse.

    10 of 10 terms
    S1 · S11
    Replace the machine with a bigger one. Simple, keeps a stateful system in one piece — and buys a restart window, a hardware ceiling, and one bigger single point of failure. A planned move, not a 2 AM one.
    S1 · S11
    Add more copies of a smaller server behind a load balancer. Near-limitless and survives one server dying, at the price of stateless design and coordination. The emergency lever and the everyday one.
    S1
    Capacity that stretches and shrinks with demand, automatically, on a meter. Ovens appear at the dinner rush and vanish at midnight, and you pay per oven-hour.
    S1 · S3
    The service that receives every request and distributes it across a pool — round-robin or least-connections. $18 a month in both course models. It spreads capacity; it never adds any.
    S3
    A probe every few seconds that lets the balancer pull a failing server out of rotation without being told. Fault tolerance arrives as a side effect of scaling out.
    S3
    Run one more server than the traffic strictly needs, so losing one changes nothing for customers. At 4,900 a minute, seven servers hit the green line and the eighth is the spare.
    S3 · S11
    The per-server load at which the group adds an instance — 700 of a rated 1,000 in the course model. Its real meaning is runway: 1,050 minus the trigger.
    S11
    Deliberate spare capacity: enough that a spike does not topple you, not so much that you become the waste statistic. 61% average utilisation is the course’s picture of healthy.
    S1
    Chopping one enormous computation into pieces run on many machines at once — SETI@home borrowed millions of idle home PCs. Coordination is not free: doubling nodes never halves the time.
    S10 · S11
    Any copy can serve any request. It is what makes scaling out possible at all, which is why a write master is the one tier that cannot follow the rule.
    In the margin

    Two rate cards live in this module and questions mix them deliberately. Session 1: 500 a minute per server, $40. Session 3: rated 1,000, green to 700, $48. Read which model you are in before you divide.

    Next Tenants and platforms
    Objectives 2 and 3 · Sessions 2, 6 and 10

    VIIIOne building, many tenants

    Two rental agreements — the finished software, or the platform under it — and one clause that keeps 900 shops apart.

    Software as a Service and Platform as a Service are one sentence read at two depths: somebody else runs the layers you decline to run. With SaaS you decline all of them and bring your data, your users and your settings. With PaaS you decline everything except the code, and the platform builds it, ships it and scales it for you. Tenancy, arithmetic, lock-in, and the AI split that closes this module are all that sentence turned into consequences.

    In the margin

    The four-part test, in order: finished application, internet delivery, provider-run stack, account or subscription. All four, or it is not SaaS.

    Plate 8 A draws the isolation the third test quietly buys you.

    Before either word is worth using, run the four-part test on the product in front of you. Is it a finished application — can a user do work immediately without deploying anything? Is it delivered over the network, through a browser or a thin client? Does the provider operate the whole stack underneath — code, servers, patches, backups, uptime? And is access tied to accounts, tenants, plans or recurring billing? A static marketing page fails three of the four. A hosted AI assistant your staff sign into with company accounts passes all four. The course’s tell is blunt: if the subscription lapsed, would you lose real work capability?

    The third test is the interesting one, because of how the provider runs one stack for everybody. Multi-tenancy means one running application and one pool of infrastructure serve many customers at once, with each tenant’s data logically isolated. BloomBase serves 900 flower shops from one deployment and one database cluster. The analogy the course uses is an apartment building: shared foundation, shared elevator, shared plumbing, one security guard — and every apartment with its own locked door. Two consequences follow. The vendor pays for the building once and divides it across every tenant, which is how a seat costs six to fifteen dollars a month. And when the elevator is upgraded — a new feature, or a security patch — every floor gets it in the same instant. No versions in the wild, nobody stranded on the 2019 build.

    Exam trap

    “Multi-tenant means my data is mixed in with my competitor’s.” No. Logically isolated is not commingled. The two legitimate worries are different ones: a noisy neighbour — Nimbus Travel’s booking season slamming shared capacity — and the blast radius when one vendor-side bug reaches all 900 tenants at once.

    But notice what the lock on that door actually is. It is not a wall, not a separate machine, not a firewall. It is a column: tenant_id on every row, and an application that adds it to the predicate of every single query. Isolation of this kind exists only where it is applied, and it is applied one statement at a time. Plate 8 A is the same table read twice.

    -- Signed in as Harbor Lane Books. The door between tenants is this predicate.
SELECT * FROM customer_records WHERE tenant_id = 'harbor';   -- 4 rows, all yours
SELECT * FROM customer_records;                              -- 8 rows, 3 tenants

    Item 8.1Objective 2Isolation

    Signed in to the vendor’s console as Harbor Lane Books, you run SELECT * FROM customer_records; and rows belonging to Gulf Coast Gym and Nimbus Travel come back beside your four. The client is watching. What does the missing clause demonstrate?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Commingling — the misconception this session exists to kill. Shared storage is not shared visibility. Every row carried its tenant_id the whole time; the statement simply declined to read it.

    • No

      Isolation confused with hardware. A dedicated instance is a cost and compliance trade, not the fix for a query that forgot its predicate — the identical bug is writable on single-tenant infrastructure.

    • Correct

      Isolation is a clause, applied one statement at a time. The safe form is WHERE tenant_id = 'harbor' and it returns four rows. Logical isolation holds exactly where the application applies it, and nowhere else.

    • No

      An encryption failure invented. Nothing about keys changed between the two statements; only the SQL did. Encryption protects bytes at rest and in flight, never a query with no predicate.

    Synthesis: multi-tenancy is cheap because the building is shared and safe because the door is checked on every entry — two properties that come from the same design and fail in different ways. Neither failure is commingled data. They are the noisy neighbour, and the blast radius of one vendor-side bug reaching all 900 tenants in the same instant.

    So the florists on Floor 4 can always buy the house next door. Single-tenancy is a dedicated instance — its own copy of the application and database, sometimes its own hardware — and vendors sell it as a premium tier to banks and hospitals. It buys real things: isolation a compliance officer can sign, room to customize, a blast radius of one. It costs a great deal more, and upgrades arrive on a schedule rather than continuously. What it does not buy is portability. Tenancy describes how customers share infrastructure; it says nothing about how your data leaves.

    Decision rule

    Prefer the product whose data you can carry. OpenSaaS is hosted, paid, supported SaaS whose underlying software is open source and whose formats are standard — WordPress.com running open-source WordPress is the pattern. Export cleanly, self-host the same stack, or move to another host running it.

    The open is in the source and in your freedom to leave. It is never in the price.

    Leaving is the sixth of the six questions that separate a buyer from a consultant: cost, data, identity, customization, reliability, exit. Amateurs ask five versions of the first one. The first is also the only one that is arithmetic, and the course fixes the method so that two consultants pricing the same decision arrive at the same number.

    Rent for thirty-six months and the total is seats × rate × 36. Own for thirty-six months and it is (seats × licence × 1.6) + hardware, where the ×1.6 bundles the perpetual licence with three years of support at twenty per cent of licence cost a year. Both columns run the same horizon or neither is a comparison. And when the two totals land within ten per cent of the larger, the course refuses to call a winner: that is a cost tie, and you decide on staffing, customization needs, cash flow and risk instead of raw dollars.

    Exam trap

    Two lines vanish from almost every student comparison: the hardware and the support contract. Drop them and owning looks like a tie it is not. The second trap is quieter — quoting the on-premises total where the question asked for the difference. A CFO catches that one in the first minute.

    Read the instrument twice. At $14 a seat there is no crossover at any seat count, because $504 of rent per seat never reaches $640 of licence and support. Move the rate to $22 and one appears at about seventy-nine seats: $792 against $640 leaves $152 a seat to work against the fixed $12,000, and the fixed cost is the entire reason a crossover exists. That single number is the most useful thing in a rent-versus-own argument, because it converts a quarrel about philosophy into a question about scale.

    Item 8.2Objective 2Arithmetic

    Marisol must present a three-year email comparison for a 120-seat client. The SaaS suite is $14 per user per month. Owning is $400 a seat in perpetual licences plus $12,000 of server hardware, with support at 20% of total licence cost a year. Using the course’s 36-month method, what are the two totals?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      Both columns complete. 120 × $14 × 36 = $60,480. (120 × $400 × 1.6) + $12,000 = $76,800 + $12,000 = $88,800. The ×1.6 is the licence plus three years of support at 20% a year.

    • No

      Support dropped. $48,000 of licences plus $12,000 of hardware is exactly $60,000 — and it omits $28,800 of support, which is the whole reason the multiplier exists.

    • No

      The horizon slipped. $50,400 is 120 × $14 × 30. Both columns run 36 months or the two numbers are not comparable at all.

    • No

      Labels swapped. The arithmetic is right and attached to the wrong columns, and $28,320 is the difference rather than either total — the slide-deck error a CFO catches instantly.

    Synthesis: one horizon, every line on both sides, and the difference reported as a difference. The number still does not end the conversation — inside ten per cent the course calls a tie and sends you to staffing, customization, cash flow and risk — but a table with a missing line is not even a place to start.

    Now decline one layer less. Deshawn’s four developers at Kettle & Crumb do not know which machine runs their ordering application, and the course’s test says they should not have to: with PaaS there is no server you can log into, because the server is not your problem. The provider runs the operating system, the language runtime, the web server, the middleware, the databases and the networking. You supply the application and its data — on the nine-layer stack, precisely the top two rows.

    The platform does three jobs, and naming only two of them is the classic exam miss. Build: detect the language, install the dependencies, run the tests, package an artifact — the same steps every time, which is how “works on my machine” dies. Deploy: start the new copy, health-check it before a customer ever reaches it, swap the router, and keep the previous version for an instant rollback. Manage: watch the load, add and remove instances, aggregate the logs, restart what crashes. The third job is where Session 1’s elasticity finally shows up on an invoice.

    [build]  Node.js 20 detected · npm ci · 214 packages in 9.8s
[build]  tests 18 passed, 0 failed · artifact harborlane-store-v1.4.2 (14.2 MB)
[deploy] web.1 up in 3.1s · GET /healthz -> 200 OK    # checked before traffic
[deploy] router swap to v1.4.2 · previous version kept for instant rollback
[scale]  spike 4x · web.2 web.3 web.4 up · p95 480ms -> 95ms
[scale]  scale-in 02:00 -> web.1              # 3 extra instances, 2 hours
    In the margin

    “PaaS means no operations” is a half-truth worth correcting out loud: you have outsourced the stage crew, not the show. Your application’s performance, its bugs, its data model and its bill are all still yours.

    What you did give up is control of runtime versions. The platform upgrades when the platform upgrades.

    That convenience is also the invoice. Platforms win your affection with proprietary conveniences — their special queue service, their custom database API, their auth SDK — and each one saves a week now and welds your application to that vendor. Vantage Freight built on all three. Two years later the renewal arrived forty per cent higher, engineers estimated seven months to run the logistics app anywhere else, and the account rep was not worried about losing the deal. He had read the same estimate.

    Item 8.3Objective 3Lock-in

    Vantage Freight’s CloudNimbus renewal lands 40% higher, and moving the logistics app elsewhere is costed at seven months because the platform’s proprietary queue, its non-standard database API and its custom auth SDK are threaded through the codebase. The CTO asks what should have been done two years ago.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Tenancy mistaken for portability. A dedicated instance changes who shares your infrastructure. Single-tenant products lock you in just as hard, because the SDKs welded into your code are the same SDKs.

    • No

      A bill confused with bargaining power. Switching autoscaling off lowers a monthly invoice and changes nothing about a seven-month rewrite — which is the only number in the room the rep is pricing.

    • No

      Too late by construction. By renewal day the leverage has already been built, and it was built into your codebase. The export clause you now want costs whatever the vendor decides it costs.

    • Correct

      Mitigations are build-time decisions. Plain SQL and standard protocols, containers and portable frameworks, vendor-specific calls behind an interface you own, and an exit estimated in dollars before the first commit.

    Synthesis: lock-in is switching cost high enough to hand the vendor pricing power, and it is accumulated one convenience at a time. The rep is calm because your own engineers wrote his negotiating position. The same paragraph will be true of a model API two sections from here — and the mitigations will not change.

    Three rental agreements, and the question each one ends with
    ModelYou supplyThe provider runsThe meterHow you would leave
    SaaS
    Workspace · a chatbot seat    		Data, users, settingsThe finished application and all nine layers under it$6–15 / seat / monthTest a full export; prefer an OpenSaaS twin you could self-host
    PaaS
    the web store · a model API    		Application code and its dataOS, runtime, web server, middleware, databases, networkingper instance · per tokenRewrite whatever speaks only this vendor’s dialect
    On-premises
    the 2016 Exchange closet    		All nine layers, and the staff for themNothing — you are the providercapital, refreshed 4–5 yrsYou already own it; the cost is migration, not exit

    Which brings the same two rental agreements to the technology everyone is currently arguing about. Strip away the chat bubble and a large language model is one function applied over and over: given all the text so far, predict the next token — a chunk of text roughly three-quarters of an English word. Nothing is looked up; everything is generated. Its working memory is the context window, and it is strictly finite, which is why VellumWorks’ support bot re-asks for a printer model the customer supplied ninety minutes earlier. Message 4 no longer fits through the reading slot. Nothing was deleted, and nothing retrained.

    Two controls sit on top of that loop. Temperature decides how often an underdog token wins the sampling — low for a billing bot, higher for brainstorming. The system prompt is invisible instructions the vendor prepends to every conversation (“You are SmileDesk. Discuss only dental topics.”), which is why Bruno’s receptionist declines celebrity gossip with no firewall involved anywhere. Read that again with this module’s first idea in mind: one shared multi-tenant model underneath, per-product behaviour set by configuration rather than custom core code. It is the apartment building with a language model in the basement.

    Exam trap

    The dearer token does not decide the lever. Output costs $0.50 a million against input’s $0.20, yet input drives 55% of the bill below, because the feature sends three times more text than it generates. Compute the share first: above 50% input, trim the prompt; below it, cap the reply.

    So the same model reaches you two ways. A chatbot subscription — a browser, a monthly per-seat bill, silent continuous updates, the provider operating every layer down to the GPUs, and millions of accounts sharing one serving fleet — is a picture-perfect SaaS product. The same models sold behind an API key are PaaS: you bring the application, you write the system prompt, and you own the token bill. That bill is arithmetic worth doing. Five thousand requests a day at 600 input and 200 output tokens, priced at $0.20 and $0.50 per million, is $0.60 of input against $0.50 of output — $1.10 a day, $33.00 a month, and a 55% input share. Measured service, priced.

    Item 8.4Objectives 2 and 3Classification

    Harbor Lane wants two AI things at once. Store managers want an assistant they sign into to draft author-event copy, billed per seat. Deshawn wants the web store to generate “customers who liked this” blurbs from inside his own code, billed per token. Classify the pair.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Whose hardware confused with what is rented. Both do run on the vendor’s GPUs; that is where the sameness ends. One is a finished application with a settings page, the other is a stage your code performs on.

    • Correct

      Both classified on the same four-part test. The assistant is finished software, reached in a browser, run wholly by the vendor, billed per seat. The API ships no application: Deshawn brings the code, writes the system prompt, pays per token.

    • No

      The platform test applied to a product. A finished chatbot contains no code of yours and offers no deployment target. Calling that PaaS empties the word of the thing it was coined to name.

    • No

      The pair inverted. Per-seat access to finished software is the SaaS shape; per-token access to a raw model your code calls is the PaaS shape. Swap them and every consequence swaps with them.

    Synthesis: the checklist never changed. Per-seat price, data handling, export rights, uptime and customization limits for the subscription; token economics, prompt portability and an abstraction layer for the API. AI lock-in is PaaS lock-in reborn, and it is mitigated with the sentences you already wrote down — standard interfaces, your own boundary around vendor calls, an exit priced from day one.

    10 of 10 terms
    S2
    One running application and one pool of infrastructure serving many customers at once, each tenant’s data logically isolated. The economic engine of SaaS: the building is paid for once and divided across every tenant.
    S2
    The isolation key: a column on every row that the application adds to the predicate of every query. Drop the clause and every tenant’s rows come back.
    S2
    A dedicated instance — its own copy of the application and database, sometimes its own hardware. More isolation and customization room; much higher cost, and upgrades on a schedule.
    S2
    One tenant’s load degrading shared performance for everyone else. Answered with quotas, throttling and capacity headroom — not with a separate building.
    S2
    Hosted, paid SaaS built on open-source software with standard formats, so you can export cleanly, self-host the same stack, or move hosts. The “open” is in the source, not in the price.
    S2 · S10
    Switching costs high enough that the vendor gains pricing power over you. Mitigated at build time or not at all: open standards, vendor code behind your own interface, the exit priced before signing.
    S2 · S6
    The seat count at which owning becomes cheaper than renting, because one fixed cost spreads over more people. ≈79 seats at $22 rented against a $400 licence and $12,000 of hardware.
    S2 · S10
    Start the new copy, health-check it, swap the router, keep the previous version. The check happens before the swap, and the old version is what makes rollback instant.
    S2
    The finite amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can attend to at once. When an early message stops fitting, it is gone from the reply — not deleted, and never retrained away.
    S2 · S10
    Invisible instructions the vendor prepends to every conversation, setting persona and guardrails. The SaaS configuration layer over one shared multi-tenant model.
    Next Renting the machine
    Objective 4 · Sessions 3 and 7

    IXRenting the machine

    Five knobs, one rate card, and a line above which every problem is yours.

    Infrastructure as a Service is the plainest bargain in the course: you rent the raw machine — cores, memory, disk, a network address, a place in the world — and you own everything from the guest operating system up. Every other decision in this module is that one sentence turned into arithmetic.

    In the margin

    The five knobs in order: how many cores, how much memory, how much disk, which of the provider’s clusters, and which operating-system image. Four of them are numbers. The fourth is also a decision about the law.

    Plate 9 A shows where the money in that line actually goes.

    The provider’s half is the physical world and the layer that slices it: data centres, power, cooling, hardware, and the hypervisor. Your half starts at the guest OS and never stops — patches, runtimes, application, data. Pelican Point Outfitters lost two virtual machines four months after migrating, through a Linux kernel hole that had been patched upstream nine weeks earlier. The provider’s hosts, network and hypervisor were demonstrably clean. The unpatched guest was theirs.

    Exam trap

    “The cloud provider manages my server.” In IaaS they manage the hardware under your server. Auto-patching exists — as an option somebody has to choose and configure. Nothing on your side of the line is automatic by definition.

    A virtual machine is ordered on five knobs: vCPU, RAM, storage, region, and image. The first three are priced, the fourth multiplies them, and the fifth is the OS snapshot the machine boots from — the one students forget is part of the specification at all. In the course rate card a core is $18 a month, a gigabyte of memory $4.50, a gigabyte of SSD $0.08, and the monthly total is (vCPU × $18 + RAM × $4.50 + GB × $0.08) × region. Divide by 730 — the standard month — for an hourly rate.

    Two of those three terms are the bill and the third is loose change. That is the first thing the plate is drawn to show, and it is why rightsizing a machine almost never touches its disk.

    Region is where the module stops being arithmetic. It sets price, it sets latency to your users, and it sets whose courts hold your data — all at once, from one dropdown. US East is the ×1.00 baseline; São Paulo at ×1.38 has historically run 30–40% above it, for the ordinary reasons that land, power, cooling, tax and network capacity are not the same everywhere. The premium is not waste when a Brazilian statute or a Frankfurt customer is buying it. It is waste when the answer to “why is this in Tokyo?” is “that is what was selected.”

    The same 8 vCPU / 64 GB / 500 GB database, priced in five regions
    RegionMultiplierMonthlyHourlyWhat buys the premium
    US East (N. Virginia)×1.00$472$0.65The baseline. Leaving it needs a reason.
    US West (Oregon)×1.04$491$0.67West-coast users, or a second region cheaply.
    Europe (Frankfurt)×1.12$529$0.72EU records that must stay in the EU.
    Asia Pacific (Tokyo)×1.20$566$0.78Users in Japan — not “it was in the list.”
    South America (São Paulo)×1.38$651$0.89Brazilian residency law. Paid on purpose.

    Item 9.1Objective 4Rate card

    Coquina Coffee Roasters runs one VM at 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 100 GB in US East — $152 a month under the course rate card. Counsel now requires EU customer records to sit in Europe (Frankfurt, ×1.12). What is the new monthly figure, and what else moved with it?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Region priced out of the formula. The multiplier is a term in the model, not a footnote to it. Latency and jurisdiction do move — and so does the invoice, on every component at once.

    • No

      Right idea, wrong rung. ×1.38 is South America and would give $210. Frankfurt is ×1.12. The ladder is 1.00 / 1.04 / 1.12 / 1.20 / 1.38, and swapping two rungs is the cheapest exam point in the course to lose.

    • Correct

      Both consequences named. $152 × 1.12 = $170.24, and the bytes now sit under EU jurisdiction, with latency to European customers improving as a bonus. Region is price, latency and law in one move.

    • No

      A discount that does not exist. No region in the model prices below the US East baseline of ×1.00 — the baseline is the floor by construction. Land, power, cooling, tax and network capacity only ever push it up.

    Synthesis: the multiplier lands on the whole line and it lands last, so changing the region changes every term you already computed. What the exam is really testing is the sentence “we just defaulted to that region” — sometimes the premium is bought deliberately, and sometimes nobody decided anything at all.

    Decision rule

    Read the ratio before the sticker price. Under 2 GB per core is a batch or encoding machine; 16 and over is a cache. A shape that does not match the role it was ordered for is either the wrong machine or the wrong role — and one of the two is about to be expensive.

    Sizing does not begin with a number. It begins with a role. A web server terminates HTTPS and hands back pages: light, stateless, the easiest thing in computing to clone. An application server runs checkout rules and coupon maths and wants more processor. A database keeps the structured truth, wants memory and a fast disk, and is the hardest thing in the building to scale because every copy must agree. A cache holds the hottest rows in memory and answers a repeat read in about a millisecond, which is how you avoid buying a bigger database. Each appetite shows up in the specification as a ratio, and the ratio is legible from the spec sheet alone.
