    Set the four knobs against the brief, say out loud what the month will cost and which knob you think binds, then commit.

    Exam trap

    Shrinking one oversized VM is rightsizing. It is not scaling out (that adds instances), not load balancing (that distributes requests), and not “more elasticity” — a fixed oversized VM is elasticity’s absence. Items pair the correct number with the wrong noun on purpose.

    The instrument is unforgiving on purpose. Every knob left one notch high bills at full price for every idle hour, because measured service charges for what is provisioned, not for what is used. Corvid Analytics’ marketing site sat on 32 vCPU / 128 GB / 200 GB — $1,168 a month — and measured 3% average CPU with a 5 GB memory peak. Rightsized to 4 vCPU / 16 GB it is $160, still with generous headroom: $1,008 a month, roughly $12,096 a year, for a machine doing exactly the same work.

    Item 9.2Objective 4Naming

    An audit at Driftwood Books finds the marketing site on 16 vCPU / 64 GB / 200 GB in US East, averaging 4% CPU. Under the rate card, what is the diagnosis, and what would moving to 2 vCPU / 8 GB / 200 GB save each month?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      Arithmetic and name together. 288 + 288 + 16 = $592; the smaller build is 36 + 36 + 16 = $88; the difference is $504 a month, about $6,048 a year, with enormous headroom still left at 4% CPU.

    • No

      The new price reported as the saving. $88 is what you will pay, not what you keep. Subtracting is the whole exercise, and this distractor exists because the two figures sit side by side on the calculator.

    • No

      The measurement dismissed. Measured demand is the entire basis of rightsizing. Throwing away the metric because it is inconvenient is precisely how a marketing site ends up on sixteen cores.

    • No

      Right money, wrong technique. Scaling out adds instances, and this machine is idle rather than overwhelmed. $504 is also the saving, not the bill — two errors travelling together.

    Synthesis: naming is graded as hard as arithmetic here. Rightsizing shrinks one machine toward measured demand; scaling out adds machines to absorb load; elasticity is capacity that follows demand with nobody typing. An option that pairs the correct number with the wrong noun is the commonest way this item is lost.

    “To be safe” is a pre-cloud reflex: when a resize took six weeks you bought for the peak you imagined. Resizing now takes minutes, so the honest posture is to size to measured demand and correct when monitoring disagrees. That requires monitoring, which is three things — metrics sampled continuously (CPU, memory, requests, latency, errors), dashboards a human glances at, and alert rules. Only the third works while everybody is asleep.

    # three rules that turn a bill into a control system
idle_vm      avg_cpu < 5% for 7d  -> ticket the owner
spend_creep  forecast > $1,500    -> email the manager
hot_fleet    cpu > 80% for 5m     -> add a server

# Opal Threads had none of them: six test VMs from a
# one-day March load test idled at 2% CPU for nine
# weeks and surfaced as $4,100 on May's statement.
# Rule one alone makes it a ~$450 lesson, in week one.

    Item 9.3Objective 4Waste

    At Tarpon Logistics a contractor starts four large test VMs for a two-day pilot and forgets them; the bill surfaces eleven weeks later, the machines averaging 3% CPU. The CIO asks for the practice that would have caught this in week one.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Waste made cheaper is still waste. A reservation lowers the rate on capacity nobody is using and commits you to it for a term. Nothing in that arrangement tells a human the machines exist.

    • No

      The surprise, scaled up. A higher region multiplier raises the price of idle capacity. Faster hardware for a pilot that ended eleven weeks ago is spending more to be wrong.

    • No

      Security answering a spend question. These VMs were forgotten, not breached. Rotation and MFA are real hygiene and entirely orthogonal — passwords never page anybody about idleness.

    • Correct

      Measured service, read by somebody. Every provisioned hour is billed, so waste appears as numbers — but only to those who look. “Flag any VM under 5% CPU for 7 days” plus “email when the monthly forecast passes $1,500” is the whole fix.

    Synthesis: the monitoring kit is metrics, dashboards and alerts, and the exam is almost always testing the third. Opal Threads paid $4,100 for nine idle weeks at 2% CPU with none of the three; the idle rule alone makes that a ~$450 lesson found in week one, before finance ever sees it.

    Objective 4 also asks you to identify solution providers, which in practice means shortlisting on friction rather than on market share. Three hyperscalers hold most of the market and sell the same three things under different names. AWS calls a VM an EC2 instance and groups them into families — m general purpose, c compute-optimised, r memory-optimised, p and g for GPUs — with EBS for block storage and ELB for balancing, across 30-plus regions. Azure sells Virtual Machines in D, E and N series and wins wherever Active Directory, Windows Server and Microsoft 365 already live. Google Cloud sells Compute Engine instances (e2, n2, a-series), brought per-second billing and automatic sustained-use discounts first, and has Kubernetes as house pedigree. Below them DigitalOcean, Linode/Akamai, Hetzner, OVH and Oracle Cloud compete on price and simplicity.

    Vendor-claim gate

    Checked 2026-07-25: Google Cloud’s Always Free e2-micro still needs a billing account and a card; Oracle verifies phone and card and may reclaim idle instances.

    Terms move. Verify the primary page before any access decision.

    Every pick carries a watch-out, and a recommendation without one is a brochure: AWS bills in hundreds of line items and charges real money to move data out; Azure’s licensing is a discipline of its own; Google Cloud’s enterprise-support ecosystem is thinner in some industries. And when the client is a student whose hard rules are $0, no payment card, and uninterrupted access for a whole term, the honest answer is that no public provider guarantees all three: AWS accounts opened on or after 15 July 2025 start with credits and a six-month free account plan rather than a blanket free tier, and every always-free offer elsewhere carries conditions. The route is an institution-provisioned Learner Lab or local compute, and the requirement gets revised rather than the risk quietly transferred to a student.

    Item 9.4Objective 4Shortlist

    Sanibel Dental Group runs Microsoft 365 and Active Directory across four offices, employs one part-time IT contractor, and wants the shortest path to a hosted line-of-business VM. What do you shortlist, and on what grounds?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Market share mistaken for fit. The catalog and the hiring pool are real advantages and neither is the constraint here. AWS’s cited watch-outs — a bill of hundreds of line items and genuine egress fees — land hardest on a client with one part-time contractor.

    • Correct

      Shortlisted on friction. Directory, licensing and identity already sit with Microsoft, and Entra ID carries straight into the identity module. Name the watch-out in the same breath: licensing complexity is Azure’s.

    • No

      A billing feature mistaken for a total. Per-second billing and automatic sustained-use discounts are real granularity wins; neither makes a per-hour rate the lowest. Google Cloud’s watch-out is a thinner enterprise-support ecosystem in some industries.

    • No

      The refusal to shortlist. Objective 4 asks you to identify providers, and the exam accepts arguments — it does not accept the absence of one. There is rarely a single right answer and there is always an unjustified one.

    Synthesis: shortlist on the friction against what the client already runs, then say the watch-out out loud — AWS bill complexity and egress, Azure licensing, Google Cloud support ecosystem. The same brief with a different incumbent produces a different provider and the same method, which is exactly what “identify solution providers” is asking you to demonstrate.

    8 of 8 terms
    S3
    Renting the fundamental resources — compute, storage volumes, networking — while the provider keeps the data centre, power, cooling, hardware and hypervisor. The customer owns the guest OS and everything above it.
    S3
    One of a provider’s data-centre clusters. Price, latency and legal jurisdiction, chosen in a single control. The multiplier is applied to the whole monthly total, last.
    S3
    The operating-system snapshot a machine boots from. The knob that is part of the specification but never part of the price.
    S3
    Matching provisioned capacity to measured demand. Shrinks one machine; adds none. $1,168 to $160 for the same marketing site is the course’s worked case.
    S3 · S1
    Every provisioned hour is billed, used or not. Waste and trouble both surface as numbers — but only to whoever is looking.
    S3
    AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud. Shortlisted on friction against the client’s incumbents, never on market share.
    S3 · S7
    A charge for moving data out of a provider, cited alongside a bill of hundreds of line items as AWS’s watch-out. Monitoring is not optional where this exists.
    S3
    Google Cloud’s automatic rate reduction for a machine that runs most of the month. Quoted with per-second billing as the granularity signal.
    Next Identity and access
    Objective 5 · Session 4

    XIdentity and access

    Move the question “who are you?” out of every application and into one professionally run service — then be honest about what that trade costs.

    Every identity system on this exam answers two questions, and students lose points by hearing one word where the course says two. Who is this user? is authentication. What may they do? is authorization. Before cloud identity, every application answered both alone: at the 12-store retail chain the course keeps returning to, a store associate touches five separate username-and-password databases — the POS register, email, the scheduling app, the HR portal, the inventory system. Multiply by 240 employees and you get the session’s own headline: one employee, twenty-three passwords, and an offboarding problem nobody can remember their way out of.

    In the margin

    Password fatigue is not laziness. It is what people do when the system asks for the impossible: they reuse, so one phished credential unlocks many systems. Between a fifth and half of all help-desk tickets are password resets, at tens of dollars of staff time each.

    See Plate 10 A for where the one surviving password is actually typed.

    Single sign-on collapses that. Maya, the chain’s new events coordinator, opens StaffMail at 9:00 on a Monday. StaffMail shows no password form of its own; it redirects her browser to CloudGate, the identity provider it trusts. She authenticates once at CloudGate — password plus an MFA push — and CloudGate issues a signed, expiring token that says, in effect, this is Maya, verified at 9:02, valid for this session. The course calls it a tamper-evident wristband from the one bouncer who actually checked ID. At 10:15 PayrollPro gets a fresh token silently, and at 11:00 so does ShiftBoard. No second login screen appears all day.

    Three things follow, and the exam wants all three. Users carry one strong credential instead of dozens. The security team gets one choke point for MFA, lockouts, anomaly detection and revocation. And the applications stop storing passwords entirely, which removes the thing an attacker was hoping to steal from each of them. The bonus nobody advertises is the kill switch: disable Maya at CloudGate and every door locks at once. Without SSO you would hunt down three separate accounts — and, as the lifecycle simulator shows, miss one.

    The honest cost is not credential concentration; it is availability. Of the seven steps in the session’s flow animator, CloudGate participates in five — steps 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 — while Maya meets it only once, at step 3. Every door she opens all day quietly checks in with the identity provider. That is why Objective 5 says appraise: uptime SLA and published outage history are evaluation criteria, not fine print. When the IdP is down, many doors stick at once.

    Exam trap

    Counting password entries. Across all seven steps and all three applications, Maya types a password exactly once, at step 3. Token handoffs are not password prompts. The companion counts: the IdP is involved in 5 of 7 steps, and IT disables 1 account to close all three apps.

    Item 10.1Objective 5Discrimination

    Maya opens StaffMail, then PayrollPro at 10:15, then ShiftBoard at 11:00 — all through CloudGate. Her manager asks the IT director exactly how many times Maya typed a password today, and where that password went.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The app treated as a password broker. A connected app that collects the password and forwards it has rebuilt the problem SSO exists to remove. Relying parties show no password form; they redirect.

    • No

      Tokens confused with a universal pass. There is no reusable “Maya token.” Every token is minted for one audience, so ShiftBoard cannot present StaffMail’s, and PayrollPro required no second password either.

    • Correct

      One authentication, many doors. The password exists in exactly one place in the company, and it is typed there once. Each app then receives its own signed, audience-locked token.

    • No

      A URL mistaken for a credential. A bookmark authenticates nobody — nothing had established who she was before step 3. What makes the later logins silent is CloudGate’s own session cookie, not the address bar.

    Synthesis: silence is not the absence of authentication, it is the reuse of one ceremony. CloudGate keeps its own session cookie; on each new app it recognises that live session and mints a fresh, differently addressed token. The login is reused; the token never is.

    Federation is the same trust, drawn across company lines. The chain’s payroll is processed by an entirely separate firm, yet employees reach the payroll site with their own CloudGate logins: the payroll firm honours CloudGate’s signed assertions and stores no retailer password at all. Gulf Coast Charters’ 85 employees reach the Dockline portal the same way, under a contract that forbids Dockline from holding a Gulf Coast password. The consumer version is the “Sign in with Google” button. Do not confuse federation with multi-tenancy — one provider serving many customers on shared infrastructure — and do not confuse it with password vaulting, which keeps an encrypted copy of the partner’s password and is precisely what federation exists to avoid.

    Three names you must be able to place — interviewers love this distinction
    StandardWhat it actually settlesWire formatWhere you meet it
    SAMLWho the user is, across company linesXML assertionsCorporate apps and older enterprise federations
    OAuth 2.0What an app may do with your dataJSON, bearer tokens“This app may read your calendar” consent screens
    OpenID ConnectWho the user is, layered on OAuth 2.0Signed JWT (ID token)Every “Sign in with Google” button today
    Exam trap

    “OAuth logs you in.” By itself it does not. OAuth 2.0 grants an app delegated access to resources; OpenID Connect is the layer that asserts who you are. Proving identity grants no resource access — reading someone’s Gmail or Drive needs separate scopes approved on a consent screen.

    Now the part the deep dive exists to correct. The session’s simplified animator says step 4 hands the browser a signed token. Production does not work that way, and the exam expects you to know both pictures and which one is recommended. In the authorization-code flow the browser carries a code — random, one-time, short-lived, bound to this client, this redirect URI and this PKCE challenge — and the real token travels server to server, over the back channel, straight into the application’s backend.

    Read the plate once more for what the redirect carries. state binds the response to this browser flow, so an attacker cannot cross-wire a login into someone else’s session. nonce makes an old ID token useless if replayed. The PKCE challenge means the code can only be redeemed by whoever created the matching secret verifier when the flow began. That is why front-channel exposure is survivable: a leaked code is short-lived, single-use, client-bound and, with PKCE, useless without a secret the browser never held.

    What comes back at step 5 is a JSON Web Token — three Base64URL parts separated by dots. The header is instructions: {"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"cg-2026-07"}, naming the signing algorithm and which published key to select after a rotation. The payload is claims: iss, sub, aud, amr, iat, exp — for Maya, subject maya-1842, audience payrollpro, issued 10:15 and expiring 10:45. The signature is tamper evidence. Note the word: encoded, not encrypted. Anyone holding the token can read it, which is fine, because possession confers no power to alter or mint one.

    # Decoding is not validating. This prints the claims and proves nothing:
echo "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | jq .
# {"iss":"https://login.cloudgate.example","sub":"maya-1842",
#  "aud":"payrollpro","amr":["pwd","mfa"],"iat":1783952100,"exp":1783953900}
# exp - iat = 1800 s = 30 min. No password appears anywhere in it:
# not encrypted, not hashed, not hidden. There never was one to carry.
    Exam trap

    “A JWT is encrypted, so the password inside it is safe.” Two errors in one sentence. The parts are encoded, and there is no password in the token. The signature buys integrity and issuer authenticity; HTTPS buys confidentiality in transit.

    PayrollPro therefore runs five checks, in order, before it will create a session: structure (three well-formed segments), issuer (the configured CloudGate issuer, not whatever iss claims), signature (bytes match the public key named by kid, fetched from CloudGate’s JWKS endpoint, using an algorithm the app allows), time (iat and exp valid at server time), and audience (aud contains payrollpro). Drop any one of them and something specific walks through the door. The bench below is that experiment.

    Bench 10 PayrollPro’s verifier 5 checks required exp ≤ 30 min

    Genuine PayrollPro tokenaud payrollpro

    realeditedalg noneexpiredaud

    Noneall five run

    nonealgsigtimeaud

    30 minutesbalanced

    5 m15 m30 m1 h2 h4 h8 h

    Checks that actually ran Awaiting commit —

    012345

    Structure · issuer · signature · time · audienceTick = all five

    Still valid after the 4:07 PM disable Awaiting commit —

    5 m30 m2 h8 h

    Log scale · 5 min → 8 hTick = the 30-minute default

    Verdict at the door — Which of the five checks stops this token, if any
    Window after revocation — Locally valid access once CloudGate says stop
    Binding check — The one input currently deciding the outcome

    Pick a token and a missing check, say out loud whether PayrollPro opens the door, then commit.

    Run the genuine token against every setting before you run the forgeries. Nothing happens. A missing audience check is invisible on every legitimate login, every day, for two years — which is exactly why it survives code review, and why “it works in production” is not evidence that a verifier is correct. The forged tokens are the only witnesses you have. Note also which library setting corresponds to which check: an allowlist of algorithms is not decoration, it is the line that refuses to let attacker-supplied text choose how the signature is verified.

    // PayrollPro's verifier — the five checks, in order, in one call
const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
  algorithms: ['RS256'],                        // never obey the token's own alg header
  issuer:   'https://login.cloudgate.example',  // the configured IdP, not the one in iss
  audience: 'payrollpro',                       // a staffmail token dies right here
  clockTolerance: 60                            // seconds of skew, not hours of grace
});                                             // malformed input throws before any of it
const userId = payload.sub;                     // identify by sub — never by email

    Item 10.2Objective 5Application

    PayrollPro’s backend receives a token that is well-formed, correctly signed by CloudGate, and not yet expired — but its aud claim reads staffmail. A junior developer wants to accept it “since the signature checks out.” What should PayrollPro do?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      The fifth check does its job. “The signature is valid, but aud says staffmail” is a rejection, not an edge case. Audience binding is what stops a compromise at one app from becoming a session at another.

    • No

      Integrity confused with authorization. A valid signature proves CloudGate wrote those bytes and nobody changed them. It says nothing about whether this application is the intended recipient.

    • No

      The IdP session misread. A live CloudGate session lets CloudGate mint a new PayrollPro token silently. It never makes another app’s token acceptable here.

    • No

      A required check demoted to metadata. Audience sits alongside issuer, algorithm, signature and expiry as a validation step. Treating it as advisory is precisely the skipped check the bench measures.

    Synthesis: the token is genuine and refused, and holding both facts at once is the whole lesson. Authenticity answers “who wrote this?”; audience answers “who was it written for?” A verifier that only asks the first question has quietly merged every connected application into one blast radius.

    Now the factor question, because a stolen password is the ordinary case. Multi-factor authentication means proofs from different categories: something you know (password, PIN, the name of your first pet — secrets in your head, and phishable), something you have (an authenticator code, a hardware key you tap, an SMS code — a physical thing, stealable but locally), something you are (fingerprint, face — convenient, and not rotatable after a compromise). Microsoft’s much-quoted finding is that MFA blocks roughly 99% of automated account-compromise attacks. Auditor Nakia’s job at Suncoast Dental is the category arithmetic: password plus security question is two knows; password plus PIN is two knows; fingerprint plus face is two ares. Only password plus authenticator code crosses a boundary.

    Exam trap

    “Two steps means two factors.” It does not. And the six-digit code from an authenticator app is a have, not a know — it proves possession of the enrolled device. The digits you type are not the secret; the device that generated them is.

    Item 10.3Objective 5Diagnosis

    Three Vantage Freight staff typed their passwords and their six-digit codes into a pixel-perfect page at vantagemail.example-support.net, which relayed both to the real site within seconds. Renata, who uses a FIDO2 security key, tried the same page and nothing happened. Why?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Strength blamed for a relay. Length changes how long an attacker must guess. It changes nothing when the user types the secret into the attacker’s form; a 40-character password is relayed as easily as a short one.

    • No

      Category error on the trap card. An authenticator code is a have — it proves possession of the enrolled device. The staff did hold two genuine factors; both were simply phishable in real time.

    • No

      The channel blamed instead of the origin. The fake site had perfectly valid TLS of its own; nothing travelled in clear text. The proxy did not intercept the session, the users handed it over.

    • Correct

      Origin binding is the whole difference. The key signs a challenge that includes the domain it is answering, so a signature produced for the lookalike domain is worthless at the real one. There is nothing for a relay to relay.

    Synthesis: the ladder is not know → have → are, it is phishable → phishing-slowing → phishing-resistant. SMS is the weakest have because SIM swap steals your phone number at a carrier counter without touching the phone; TOTP buys thirty seconds, which a live proxy spends comfortably; only an origin-bound credential removes the attack rather than timing it.

    Decision rule

    Require the strongest factor the population can actually carry: FIDO2 keys or passkeys first, an authenticator app second, SMS last and flagged as weak. Then budget for the recovery path — a lost key with no recovery is an outage you built yourself.

    Tokens expire, and this is where students over-claim in both directions. Disabling Maya at CloudGate at 4:07 PM stops new tokens immediately. It does not reach into PayrollPro and cancel the one issued at 4:02, because a self-contained JWT is validated without ever calling its issuer — that is the property that makes it fast, and the same property that makes it unrecallable. Short lifetimes bound the damage; systems that need faster shutdown add introspection, denylists, token-version claims, security-event notifications, or coordinated app-session revocation. Run the second gauge on the bench at four hours and read the sentence it prints: four hours of locally valid access after the identity provider has said stop.

    Five clocks inside one smooth login — illustrative lifetimes, not a promise from any provider
    CredentialWhat it is forIllustrative lifeWhat its expiry does not do
    ID tokenTells one app who authenticated60 minDoes not sign the user out of that app
    Access tokenAuthorizes API calls within its scope60 minDoes not end the app’s own session
    Refresh tokenMints replacement access tokensdaysDoes not keep a screen signed in by itself
    App session cookieKeeps the website signed in7 daysDoes not disappear when Google is signed out
    Google account sessionLets Google re-issue without a password30 daysDoes not delete the app’s own cookie

    Item 10.4Objective 5Appraisal

    CloudGate disables a departing employee’s account at 4:07 PM. The vendor’s default token lifetime is eight hours “for SSO convenience.” The security lead asks what actually happens to that person’s access at 4:08 PM.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The kill switch over-claimed. This is the comforting myth the lifetime lab exists to kill. Instant global revocation is something you must buy with introspection, denylists or token-version checks — it is not free with SSO.

    • Correct

      The honest lag, stated. A self-contained token is validated without calling its issuer, so the issuer cannot pull back every copy. An eight-hour default turns a disgruntled exit into an all-day incident.

    • No

      Introspection assumed, not configured. Per-request re-checking is a real design — and precisely the design a self-contained JWT flow avoids for speed. If you want it, you specify it and you pay the round trip.

    • No

      A mechanism invented. exp is enforced by the verifying application at validation time, not by CloudGate, and password rotation has nothing to do with the life of an already-issued token.

    Synthesis: the kill switch is real and it is bounded. Disabling the account closes the issuing door immediately and leaves already-open doors closing on their own schedule, so the offboarding SLA you can actually promise is the token lifetime you configured — which is why the course’s balanced default is thirty minutes and why “eight hours for convenience” is a security decision wearing a usability costume.

    Which brings the lifecycle into view, because most real findings are not cryptographic at all. Provisioning creates accounts and entitlements when someone joins or changes role; deprovisioning revokes them when someone leaves. The course names the asymmetry precisely. Joiners are self-correcting — a new hire without email complains, loudly, until access appears. Movers fail quietly: a promotion adds rights and almost never removes the old ones, which is privilege creep. Leavers fail silently and permanently, because nobody ever complains about an account that should be dead but is not. In the simulator’s manual universe, Maya’s Friday 4:00 PM resignation disables email on Monday morning and leaves behind three findings: a POS account a helpful shift lead used two weeks later, an uncollected VPN token the auditors dial in with during the exit briefing, and a Dropbox share invited to her personal email, still syncing price lists. In the automated universe, one HR termination event at 4:07 PM closes everything, logged seven minutes after HR’s entry, with zero findings.

    Exam trap

    “Deprovisioning means deleting the account.” Best practice is disable immediately, delete later. Disabling kills access instantly while preserving mail, files and the audit trail — the exact evidence you need for the investigation an orphaned account triggers.

    Item 10.5Objective 5Discrimination

    An access review finds that Maya, promoted from sales associate to store manager two years ago, still holds every associate-only entitlement alongside her inventory-admin, payroll-approval and scheduling-admin rights. Nobody has ever complained. Classify the failure.

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      The wrong stage of the lifecycle. Joiner failures are about arrival delay — the week Maya waited for a POS login. They cost money, they generate complaints, and they get fixed for exactly that reason.

    • No

      “Leaver” stretched to cover a role change. Maya has not left. Leaver failures are the doors still open after a departure: the POS account, the VPN token, the Dropbox share.

    • Correct

      Textbook privilege creep. Adds happen because someone complains when access is missing; removals do not, because nobody complains about extra access. Two years of promotions produce the union of every job you have held.

    • No

      Orphan misapplied. An orphaned account is a live credential with no living owner. These rights sit on Maya’s own legitimate, actively used account — which is precisely what makes them so hard to see.

    Synthesis: sort lifecycle failures by who complains. Joiner failures cost money and are self-correcting. Mover and leaver failures cost security and are self-concealing, so they surface in the audit rather than the ticket queue — which is the whole argument for making the HR system the system of record and letting one event fan out to every application.

    Decision rule

    Make the HR system the system of record and let one joiner/mover/leaver event fan out to every application. Then keep reviewing access, because automation shrinks the manual list — it does not abolish it. The Dropbox share invited to a personal email is wired to nothing.

    Adaptive authentication is the reason modern MFA does not nag every five minutes. The platform scores each login on device fingerprint, network, geography, time of day and typing cadence, then spends friction where risk lives: Maya on her usual laptop at her usual store on a Tuesday morning sails through; a brand-new phone triggers a step-up; and a Tampa session at 1:58 AM followed by the same account from an IP 5,100 miles away at 2:14 is blocked outright as impossible travel. Security teams call behaviour the emerging fourth factor, something you do. Note what caught the Palmetto Provisions intrusion: both classic factors passed — the password and the code were stolen intact — and the behavioural layer is what noticed a password typed 40% slower than the stored rhythm profile.

    Finally, the appraisal itself, because Objective 5 says appraise and Milestone 2 asks you to justify an identity choice with three criteria. The checklist is fixed: protocol support (SAML and OIDC), the size of the pre-built application catalogue, HR connectors for lifecycle automation, MFA options including phishing-resistant factors, uptime SLA and published outage history, admin and reporting quality, and per-user price at your headcount. Ridgeline Hardware’s quote of $6 per user per month is about $17,000 a year for 240 people, and the build-it-ourselves alternative is a specialist, high-stakes function one generalist cannot build, patch and monitor alone. When a salesperson says “five nines guaranteed forever, and we make phishing impossible,” the professional answer is neither acceptance nor refusal: ask for the SLA text and its remedies, the outage history, and the list of factors that are actually origin-bound.

    20 of 20 terms
    S4
    Proving who a user is. Answered once, at the identity provider.
    S4
    Determining what an authenticated user may do. Privilege creep is a failure of this half, never of the first.
    S4
    One authentication at a trusted provider; every connected app accepts its signed token instead of running a login of its own.
    S4
    The service that authenticates the person, writes the claims, signs with its private key, publishes its public keys, and decides whether new tokens may be issued.
    S4
    A connected application that stores no password and validates the IdP’s token before creating its own session.
    S4
    Independent organisations trusting each other’s signed assertions, so a partner never stores your passwords. Not multi-tenancy; not password vaulting.
    S4
    Delegated authorization — “this app may read my calendar.” It does not, by itself, say who you are.
    S4
    The identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0; what actually powers “Sign in with Google” today.
    S4 · deep dive
    Header, payload and signature, dot-separated and Base64URL encoded, not encrypted. A format, not a guarantee.
    deep dive
    The single client a token was minted for. A StaffMail token is refused at PayrollPro however valid its signature.
    deep dive
    Header fields naming the signing algorithm and which published key to select after a rotation. The app enforces its own allowlist rather than obeying alg.
    deep dive
    Where an app fetches the IdP’s public keys. A public key can check a signature; it can never create a new valid one.
    deep dive
    A random, single-use, short-lived value bound to the client, the redirect URI and the PKCE challenge — carried by the browser, redeemed by the backend.
    deep dive
    Proof Key for Code Exchange: redeeming the code requires the secret verifier created when the flow began.
    deep dive
    Front channel = messages carried through the browser by redirect; back channel = direct server-to-server HTTPS. The token takes the back channel.
    deep dive
    A credential that works for anyone holding it. The signature prevents edits, not copying — which is why lifetime is a security control.
    S4
    The signature includes the domain being answered, so a response produced on a lookalike site is worthless at the real one.
    S4
    The identity lifecycle: access arrives, access changes, access ends. Only the first stage generates complaints.
    S4
    A live credential with no living owner — among the most common findings in real security audits.
    S4
    Demanding another factor mid-session when risk rises or a sensitive area opens — friction spent where it is earned.
    Decision rule

    Buy identity, do not build it. The subscription buys SSO, MFA, HR connectors, anomaly detection and an uptime SLA. It does not buy role design, access policy, MFA rules or offboarding discipline — those stay yours, permanently.

    Next Storage: shape, tier, copies
    Objective 6 · Session 5

    XIStorage: shape, tier, copies

    Three questions asked in a fixed order — what shape the data wants, what tier its access pattern earns, and how many genuinely independent copies exist.

    Every storage question on this exam is one of three questions wearing a business costume. What shape does this data want — block, file, or object? What tier does its access pattern earn — hot, cool, or archive? How many copies exist, and do they share a roof? Students lose points by answering them out of order: they pick a tier from a price sheet before they know how often the data is read, or they count copies before they ask where the copies live.

    Start with the history, because it is one story and not four definitions. Direct-attached storage put disks inside one machine. Network-attached storage moved them onto an appliance the whole office could reach. A storage area network moved them onto a dedicated fabric the data centre’s servers could share. Cloud storage moved them out of your building entirely and put a meter on them. Each era decoupled the data from one more thing: DAS to NAS freed it from one person’s machine, NAS to SAN freed it from one server, and cloud freed it from one address.

    In the margin

    Dr. Okafor’s fourteen years of imaging sit on drives 91% full inside one machine, and an X-ray reboot blacks out the practice for forty minutes. Adding a second server does not fix that. It buys a second island.

    See Plate 11 A for what each shape actually sends across the wire.

    That history matters because it explains the one distinction the exam tests most often. A NAS and a SAN are not two words for shared storage. A NAS speaks file protocols — SMB and NFS — and the client asks for a whole file by name: give me /invoices/march.pdf. A SAN speaks Fibre Channel or iSCSI, and the client asks for numbered sectors: give me sectors 4096–8191. The abstraction is the difference. Hand an accountant’s workstation a raw block volume and it does not see the shared drive it wanted; it sees an unformatted disk.

    Forty years of moving data one step farther from a single machine
    EraYearsWhat it decoupledSurvives today as
    DAS1980s–90sNothing yet — data welded to one machine’s fateYour laptop’s SSD, and the disks inside every cloud server
    NASmid-1990sData from one user’s machineOffice shared drives, home appliances, cloud file services
    SANlate 1990s–2000sData from one serverCloud block storage — “EBS is SAN as a service”
    Cloud2006 →Data from your buildingThe default for everything new, billed per GB-month

    The cloud kept both of those abstractions and added a third. Block storage hands one virtual machine a raw volume of numbered chunks and lets the operating system impose a filesystem on it. File storage hands many clients a ready-made filesystem with paths and permissions. Object storage hands anything with an HTTP client a whole blob addressed by a key. Choose by what the workload has to read and write, never by the nouns in the scenario — the word “file” in “photo file” is not a vote for file storage.

    Copperleaf Market’s point-of-sale backend rewrites thousands of small pieces of its PostgreSQL data files every minute. On block storage that is thousands of small in-place writes. In a bucket it is thousands of whole-object re-uploads over HTTP, which is why the “23× cheaper per GB” argument collapses the moment you ask what a single sale costs. The rule is short: block for the live database, object for its backups.

    Exam trap

    “Raw block volume” does not mean unencrypted. Raw is a statement about structure — the service supplies addressable blocks and imposes no file or folder scheme. The operating system supplies NTFS or ext4; encryption is a separate control entirely.

    The same discipline kills the other favourite distractor. An object key such as covers/2026/book.jpg contains slash characters that look like folders, but the namespace is flat — there is no directory tree to lock or rebalance, which is exactly why a bucket scales to billions of objects while a hierarchical file share starts wheezing at StreetSnap’s two million photos.

    Item 11.1Objective 6Discrimination

    Copperleaf Market’s cloud POS commits every sale to PostgreSQL, rewriting thousands of small pieces of its data files every minute. A junior architect wants the live database files hosted in object storage because it is “23× cheaper per GB than the disks we rent.” On what grounds do you overrule him?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Durability invented as the objection. Backwards: a multi-zone object store is usually the durability champion of the whole catalogue. Reaching for “it might lose data” is what a student does when the real mechanism has not been named.

    • No

      Regulation mistaken for a technology ban. PCI-DSS governs how cardholder data is protected and retained. It does not outlaw cloud databases — thousands of banks run them under it.

    • Correct

      Write granularity, named exactly. A database engine seeks and rewrites small regions inside big open files and needs sub-millisecond block I/O. Changing one byte of an object means re-uploading the whole object over HTTP.

    • No

      A size limit invented from nowhere. Object stores routinely hold multi-terabyte objects. The blocker is never how big one object may be; it is that you cannot edit inside one.

    Synthesis: price per GB is the last question, not the first. Plate 11 A’s third row settles this in one glance — block re-inks a chunk, object re-inks everything — and the correct architecture keeps both: block for the live database, object for the nightly backups it writes out. The cheap tier is right for the copy and wrong for the original.

    Now the second question, and the one clients get wrong in public. Durability and availability are different promises with different mathematics. Durability asks whether the bytes still exist and is quoted as a loss probability: eleven nines means that if you store ten million objects you should expect to lose one in roughly ten thousand years. Availability asks whether you can reach those bytes right now, and it is quoted separately, and lower, around 99.9x%. Nobody sells eleven-nines availability.

    Exam trap

    “Eleven nines, so we’re basically never down.” No. That figure is a loss probability, not an uptime figure, and it converts to no number of seconds per year. A provider outage can leave perfectly durable data briefly unreachable — annoying, not fatal.

    The third pairing is the one this course promises will appear in bold. Replication is not backup. Replication keeps current copies alive on separate devices so hardware failure is invisible; it also copies deletions, corruption and ransomware with the same enthusiasm, because its whole job is to make every copy identical fast. Versioning preserves older states so you can rewind. Three healthy replicas of a deleted object are three healthy nothings.

    And replication itself has a second trap, which is geographic rather than numerical. Three copies protect you only if the three failures are independent. Spread them across availability zones — separate buildings with their own power and network — and the provider quietly re-syncs a fresh copy from the survivors in a couple of seconds. Stack them in three racks of one suite and a single flood is a single failure with three casualties.

    Item 11.2Objective 6Client-facing

    At the pitch, Beacon Bicycles’ owner reads the vendor slide aloud — “product images stored with 99.999999999% durability” — and asks whether eleven nines means the storefront essentially never goes offline. Consultant Jocelyn gets one sentence. Which one is right?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Durability read as uptime. The most common version of this error. A loss probability has no conversion into seconds of downtime; it says how unlikely you are to lose an object, not how often you can reach it.

    • No

      Numerology. The nines are decimal places in a probability, not a count of anything. Encryption is a confidentiality control and is orthogonal to whether bytes survive or answer.

    • No

      The consultant’s dodge. The figure is estimated from published replication design and device failure statistics. Calling a number you have not examined “marketing” is how a consultant loses the room.

    • Correct

      Two promises, two numbers. Durability is a loss probability — ten million objects, one loss in roughly ten thousand years. Availability is reachability now, quoted separately and always lower.

    Synthesis: when a slide quotes one of these numbers, ask for the other, because they are bought with different mechanisms. Copies and independent failure domains buy durability; capacity, failover and multi-zone front ends buy availability. A client who hears “eleven nines” and plans no failover has bought a guarantee that the bytes will outlive the outage they are about to have.

    Item 11.3Objective 6Threat matching

    Ransomware encrypts every file on Coastal Realty’s office server at 6:14 AM Friday. Denise says the firm is fine because the folder syncs to a cloud drive — but the sync client uploaded each encrypted file within seconds. Which single capability would have rescued them?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      More perfect copies of the attack. Replication answers “a device died,” never “a change was bad.” Two more regions means the encrypted files are now beautifully protected in three places.

    • Correct

      History, not copies. Versioning keeps prior states, so the share rolls back to 6:13 AM. Sync cannot help, because replicating every change faithfully is exactly what it is for.

    • No

      RAID mistaken for a time machine. RAID addresses disk hardware failure only. It will faithfully store encrypted garbage with excellent redundancy and no opinion about it.

    • No

      A tier confused with a control. Archive changes price and restore latency, not history. An encrypted file in archive is cheaper encrypted garbage that also takes hours to fetch.

    Synthesis: match the mechanism to the threat. Device failure or an unreachable site is replication’s job; a bad change — deletion, corruption, ransomware, a stolen admin credential — is versioning’s, and immutability is what stops the attacker deleting the versions too. That is why the “1” in 3-2-1 wants to be offline or under object lock, and why separating backup credentials from production credentials is an identity control doing storage work.

    Only now does price belong in the conversation. Tiers do not price space alone; they price access. Hot storage costs the most per terabyte, answers immediately, and charges little or nothing to read. Cool costs less and adds retrieval charges and minimum-duration rules. Archive is nearly free to hold, takes hours to restore, and charges steeply per terabyte thawed. That last fee is where the exam lives.

    The three tiers on this course’s model prices, rounded from public rate cards
    TierStorageRetrievalRestore waitChoose when the data is
    Hot$23 / TB·molittle or noneimmediateused daily or hourly — active databases, live site assets
    Cool$12 / TB·mocharges applyimmediateused monthly — older projects, infrequent reports
    Archive$1 / TB·mo$30 / TB restoredhoursrarely opened but must be retained — compliance records
    Exam trap

    “Archive tiers quietly delete data after ninety days.” They do not. They impose minimum storage durations with early-deletion fees — the opposite of silent deletion. The archive risks are a retrieval bill and an hours-long wait, never a vanished object.

    TrendMart’s CFO read “$1 a terabyte,” moved all sixty terabytes to archive, and now thaws ten terabytes a month for the analytics team. Set the bench below to his plan and then to yours. The dials stay dark until you commit, because the point of the instrument is to make you predict the bill before you read it.

    Bench 11 TrendMart · one 60 TB corpus All-hot baseline $1,380/mo Archive restore $30/TB

    0 TB hot60 TB archive

    0102030405060

    10 TB restored$30 per TB

    025101520

    Monthly bill Awaiting commit —

    $0$500$1,000$1,600

    Linear · $0 to $1,600Tick = the all-hot bill

    Retrieval share Awaiting commit —

    0%25%50%75%100%

    Decision rule

    If retrieval fees exceed the archive storage line, the data is not cold. Classify by access pattern first, then tier — never the reverse. Promoting the frequently-thawed slice raises a bounded storage line; leaving it raises an unbounded fee that scales with demand.

    Item 11.4Objective 6Arithmetic

    TrendMart’s CFO parked all 60 TB in archive at $1 per TB-month and thaws 10 TB every month for analysts. You propose 10 TB hot plus 50 TB archive with no routine restores. On the model prices, what does “archive everything” cost?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      The retrieval line carried the bill. Archive-everything is 60 × $1 plus 10 × $30 = $360. The split is 10 × $23 plus 50 × $1 = $280. The gap is $80, and every dollar of it is retrieval.

    • No

      The comparison inverted. The hot line is what makes the split cheaper overall, not more expensive. $130 is a plausible-looking number with no arithmetic behind it.

    • No

      Headline price mistaken for total price. This is the exact myth the exercise exists to kill. The per-GB discount on cold tiers is subsidised by the retrieval fee you pay when you misjudge the access pattern.

    • No

      One restore counted, ten performed. The plan thaws ten terabytes a month, not one. Reading the unit price and forgetting the quantity is the arithmetic slip this scenario is built around.

    Synthesis: he chased a 95% discount on the storage line and bought a 29% bigger bill. The general rule the bench draws for you is the break-even: once you restore roughly 70–75% of an archive every month, the cheap tier is an expensive hot tier that also makes you wait hours. Tiering is worth real money — on a media split of 8 hot, 40 cool and 200 archive it saves $4,780 a month — but only when the access assumption is honest.

    Copies come last, and the rule is 3-2-1: three copies of anything that matters, on two different media or services, with one held offsite and ideally immutable or offline. Nine Elms’ retail plan reads live database, nightly versioned backup in object storage, weekly export into an immutable archive bucket under object lock. Three supporting habits make it real — versioning so you can rewind before an attack, a tested restore because a backup is only proven when you have restored it, and separated access so stolen production credentials cannot erase every backup.

    aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket nineelms-share \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled   # the only line here that answers ransomware

aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket tworivers-ledger \
  --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled",
    "Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Mode":"COMPLIANCE","Days":2555}}}'
# 2555 days = 7 years. COMPLIANCE means the admin credential cannot shorten it either.

    Two Rivers Coffee needs financial records held seven years, producible for auditors within a day or two, opened maybe twice a year, and provably unalterable after a franchise lawsuit. Each requirement names a feature: the seven years is a retention policy, the twice-a-year access with day-scale tolerance is the archive tier, and “provably unalterable” is object lock. A NAS with a note asking staff not to edit the records folder fails outright, because a sticky note is not a control.

    All of which is why the design starts before the architecture. List every data set — database, uploads, static assets, logs, config, backups — and only then assign each one a shape, a tier, a region, a retention period and an access list. That classification register is the exhibit that makes a storage plan defensible, and it is what forces the compliance columns nobody volunteers to fill in. Note that no regulation bans a technology: HIPAA and PCI-DSS govern protection, retention, residency and access, not cable type.

    One shape has been added to the catalogue recently, and it belongs here rather than in an AI chapter. An embedding turns text or an image into coordinates of meaning, so “return policy” lands near “refunds and exchanges” without sharing a word; a vector database stores those coordinates and answers “what is closest in meaning?” across millions of them. Retrieval-augmented generation is therefore a storage architecture before it is a model decision — originals in cheap object storage, the meaning index in the vector database, linked by shared keys — which is how Cielo Insurance’s assistant quoted a policy published twenty minutes earlier, with a citation. Uploading a document changes storage and the index; it never touches the model’s parameters.

    12 of 12 terms
    S5
    Raw numbered blocks presented to one virtual machine like a disk; the operating system adds the filesystem. Low latency, one server at a time.
    S5
    A ready-made shared filesystem with folders, paths and permissions that many clients mount at once. Speaks SMB or NFS.
    S5
    Whole blobs stored with metadata under a unique key and reached over HTTP. Cheapest per GB, effectively unlimited, no in-place edits.
    S5
    The unique name of an object. Slashes in it are characters that look like folders — the namespace is flat, with no directory tree to lock or rebalance.
    S5
    Will the bytes still exist? A loss probability: store ten million objects and expect one loss in roughly ten thousand years.
    S5
    Can you reach the data right now? A separate and always lower number. Durable data can be temporarily unreachable.
    S5
    Current copies kept alive on separate devices, usually in separate zones, so hardware failure is invisible — and so are deletions, faithfully copied.
    S5
    Point-in-time states preserved so you can rewind after a mistake or an attack. The one capability replication cannot provide.
    S5
    A separate building with its own power and network inside a region. Spreading replicas across zones is what makes a site disaster survivable.
    S5
    The per-terabyte charge for reading data out of a cool or archive tier — the fee that turns a cheap tier expensive when the access pattern is wrong.
    S5
    Write-once-read-many retention with a clock that not even the admin credential can override until it expires. The proper form of the “1” in 3-2-1.
    S5
    A store of embeddings that finds the nearest matches by meaning. Consulted on every request, so it is the hottest data in the system, never archive.
    Decision rule

    Before counting copies, count failure domains. Ask of each copy: does it share a roof, a power feed, a flood plain, or an administrator credential with another copy? Copies that answer yes to any of those are one copy with extra steps.

    Next Traveling copies and one master copy
    Objective 6 · Session 6

    XIIOne copy of the truth

    Where the document lives, when the humans must be in the same minute, and what the meeting actually costs.

    Every collaboration tool answers one question before it answers any other: where does the document live? Email sends copies to the people. The cloud sends the people to the copy. Nearly everything else in this module — version chaos or version history, the Saturday merge or no merge at all — follows from that single architectural choice, which is why the exam asks you to name the model before it asks you to name a product.

    In the margin

    Say it once and it survives the exam: email sends the file to the people; the cloud sends the people to the file. Six recipients, six forks. One master, no forks — because there is nothing to fork.

    See Plate 12 A for the two models drawn side by side.

    Watch the fork happen. Pelican Outfitters mailed Budget.xlsx to six department heads. Fourteen reply-attachments came back, thirty cells disagreed across the copies, and a controller spent a full Saturday reconciling them by hand. One change never made it into the reconciled file, and it surfaced in the board meeting. Nobody was careless. The store-and-forward model did exactly what it is built to do: it relayed a copy, and the moment a copy exists in two hands it is two documents.

    Exam trap

    “A naming convention would have fixed it.” No. Budget_v7_MK_0411 and Budget_v7_SR_0411 are still two documents; the names are just tidier. The disease is the traveling copy, and no discipline applied after the fork can merge it. The same goes for a bigger attachment limit, which treats the mailbox for a problem the mailbox did not cause.

    The shared-master model buys exactly three observable things, and they are the evidence you look for when a scenario refuses to name the product. Co-editing with presence: simultaneous edits merge at keystroke granularity and coloured cursors show who is working where — no file-lock dialog, no overwrite. Comments, @mentions and suggesting mode: review happens inside the artifact, where a proposed sentence can be accepted or rejected, instead of around it in a reply-all thread. Version history: a time machine with a name and a timestamp on every change, which is what finally kills Final_v9_REALfinal2.docx.

    Exam trap

    Version history and co-editing get swapped constantly. Version history explains recovering the past; co-editing is the merged present. When Ruth and Desmond edit hardcover and paperback prices in the same Cormorant Books master list at 4:55 PM from stores forty miles apart, with live cursors and no lock dialog, that is co-editing. A nightly sync would have delivered the truth seven hours after the 5 PM promotion started.

    Item 12.1Objective 6Discrimination

    After the Pelican Outfitters budget cycle — six mailed copies, fourteen reply-attachments, thirty conflicting cells and a change that reached the board meeting missing — the CFO asks for the fix that prevents a repeat. What do you tell her?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      Tidier names, identical forks. A convention labels copies; it cannot merge them. v7-Susan and v7-Marcus still disagree in thirty cells, and the discipline collapses in the first busy week. This is the most popular wrong answer in the course because it feels like process improvement.

    • No

      The mailbox blamed for the model. Nothing here failed because of file size. Store-and-forward relays a copy by design, so a larger limit simply lets bigger forks travel faster.

    • No

      Check-out mistaken for collaboration. Locking does prevent divergence — by preventing concurrency. Five heads wait, the budget cycle serialises, and you have solved the merge by abolishing the collaboration.

    • Correct

      The fork made impossible. One master in the cloud means there are no copies to diverge; the service merges at keystroke granularity, and version history keeps the past retrievable instead of scattered across inboxes.

    Synthesis: three of these four answers accept the traveling-copy architecture and try to manage its symptoms — naming them, enlarging them, or serialising access to them. Only one changes where the document lives. When a scenario describes reconciliation work, ask what would have to be true for reconciliation to be unnecessary; the answer is always a single master.

    Now the second decision, and it is independent of the first: when do the humans have to be in the same minute? Synchronous work is same time, instant back-and-forth, expensive attention. Asynchronous work is own time, documented, time-zone-proof. Nova Analytics runs a 9:00 AM Denver standup whose content is ninety per cent “did, will do, blockers” — which lands at 11 PM in Manila and 5 PM in Warsaw. That is an async-shaped ritual being run in sync mode, and the cost is paid in the two time zones that cannot argue back.

    Exam trap

    Async is not the enlightened default. Teams fail in both directions: meetings that should have been documents, and week-long comment wars that needed one ten-minute call. A hard performance conversation and a production outage are sync; a twenty-page architecture critique and an end-of-day handoff are async.

    The tell is never the topic and never the artifact. Keep the memo, the people and the subject identical and move only the clock, and the same conversation flips mode: a Cormorant Books comment thread that was resolving beautifully over two days becomes a call the moment the landlord’s agent needs a yes in forty-five minutes. Bench 12 A makes that flip computable. It estimates how long the asynchronous path actually takes — one review round-trip for the people you need, multiplied by the number of exchanges the work requires — and holds it against the time left on the clock. Above 100 per cent the thread cannot converge before the deadline, and that is when you buy synchronous time; the second gauge prices what you are about to buy in person-hours.

    Decision rule

    If the work dies without instant back-and-forth, buy sync. If it only needs a durable record someone can read on their own clock, write the artifact. Urgency and stakes decide; the topic never does. Notice which dial the instrument almost never blames: adding people barely moves the async path, because async is the mode that parallelises across humans.

    Item 12.2Objective 6Application

    Cormorant Books has been arguing in comments on the lease-renewal memo for two days, and it is going well: considered, documented, no meeting needed. Then the landlord’s agent calls — a yes or no in forty-five minutes or the space goes to another tenant. Same memo, same people, same topic. What now?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • No

      A default mistaken for a principle. Async was the right mode for two days and is the wrong mode for forty-five minutes. A thread that resolves “over two days” is precisely the thing that cannot resolve now.

    • Correct

      The clock moved, so the mode moves. Nothing about the artifact, the people or the topic changed — only the deadline — and urgency is what buys expensive simultaneous attention. Three deciders, one call, record written afterwards.

    • No

      Async at the wrong speed. End of day is after the deadline. Choosing the right mode and then missing the clock is the same failure as choosing the wrong mode.

    • No

      Audience confused with decision. Eight more voices add inbox-shaped delay to a decision that needs three people and one conversation. Completeness of the record is a job for the write-up, not for the invite list.

    Synthesis: this is the flip test, and it is the single sentence to carry into the midterm — “should this be a meeting?” is answered by the clock and the stakes, never by the topic. Two of the wrong answers are async done badly and one is async defended on principle; the exam usually offers you at least one of each.

    Choosing tools is a different discipline again, and it is where consultants earn their fee, because every vendor demo looks wonderful. Six criteria sit behind the gloss. Cost — free tiers are real but have real edges: Zoom Basic cuts a call at forty minutes, Slack’s free plan hides messages after ninety days, which is why chat on a free tier is a poor system of record. Integration and SSO. Data export. Security and compliance. Adoption and training — the best tool nobody opens loses to the decent tool everyone already knows. Vendor viability — will this company, and your data inside it, exist in five years? Four of those are scored and traded off against each other. Two of them are walls.

    The six selection criteria, the question each one asks, and what failing it costs
    CriterionThe question it asksFailing it costs youShape
    CostWhere does the free tier stop?Calls cut at 40 minutes; chat gone after 90 daysScored
    Integration & SSOCan it federate with the one identity provider?A manual account opened and closed for every hire and departureGATE
    Data exportCan we leave with messages, files and recordings?Lock-in applied to your own meeting and chat historyGATE
    Security & complianceWhere does the data sit, and who may export it?A retention rule you cannot satisfy on paperScored
    Adoption & trainingWill anyone actually open it?Licences paid for a tool the work routes aroundScored
    Vendor viabilityWill this company exist in five years?Your data inside somebody else’s shutdown noticeScored
    Exam trap

    Two disguises for the same error. The first is weighting the six criteria and letting a total decide — that treats a veto as a preference. The second is worse: adopting the non-SSO tool and having people reuse their single-sign-on password so the login “still matches.” That spreads the crown-jewel credential outside the identity provider’s protection, which is the exact anti-pattern SSO exists to end.

    Item 12.3Objective 6Judgement

    At Tidewater Markets — 240 employees, twelve stores, heavy seasonal turnover — Priyanka brings back a meetings tool that tops every feature chart and undercuts the incumbent on price. It cannot federate with the company identity provider, and it offers no export of recordings or chat. What is your recommendation?

    Debrief · every option, named

    • Correct

      A gate is a veto, not a weight. No federation means a manual account provisioned and — the dangerous half — deprovisioned by hand for every one of 240 seasonal hires and leavers. No export means your own meeting history is hostage. Failing either is disqualifying; failing both is not a close call.

    • No

      The credential spread by hand. Reusing the identity-provider password in a tool the provider does not control puts the crown jewels outside every protection SSO gives you, and a departure now leaves an account nobody can close.

    • No

      A veto made to wait for a rival. Disqualification does not depend on the alternatives. “Adopt now, fix identity later” is how chart-topping tools get in and then cannot be deprovisioned.

    • No

      Gates traded off as preferences. Weighting lets a brilliant feature score outvote a missing control. That is precisely the arithmetic the two hard gates exist to forbid.

    Synthesis: run the gates before the scoring, not after. Four criteria compose — a cheap tool can pay for weaker training, a beloved tool can pay for a higher price — and two do not compose at all. The professional sentence is short: great features, fails the gates, pass.

    That is also the honest answer to suite versus best-of-breed. A suite buys one login, interlinked files, calendar and meetings, and one admin console; a best-of-breed stack buys the strongest individual features and owes an integration plan — five logins unless every tool federates, five notification streams, five admin consoles, five export policies. But no suite covers everything. Across Wayfarer Studio’s five needs, a single vendor reaches four; the whiteboard row has no suite option at all, so the seam is structural, not a planning failure. And more tools is not more collaboration: Brightwave Media adopted chat, a project board, a wiki, a meetings tool and kept email — five best-in-category products — and six months later decisions lived in threads nobody could find, the wiki contradicted the board, and response times were worse than before.

    Decision rule

    The fix for sprawl is subtraction and agreements, never addition. Consolidate, then name one system as the source of truth and say what each surviving channel is for: decisions live on the board, chat is ephemeral, the wiki is reference. A sixth tool that searches the other five is a sixth inbox.

    Now price the sync time you decided to buy. A meeting is a purchase that never sends an invoice, and the model is small enough to do in your head: cost = attendees × loaded hourly rate × duration ÷ 60, where the loaded rate is salary plus benefits plus overhead — what an hour truly costs the employer. Multiply by 52 for anything weekly. Wayfarer Studio’s Monday all-hands is fourteen people at $60 an hour for sixty minutes: $840 an occurrence, $43,680 a year, a mid-range salary that never appeared in a budget review. Cutting the invite to the six people who actually speak makes it $360 and $18,720 — $24,960 saved with one edit to a calendar invite. The calculator is not anti-meeting. A $600 decision meeting that prevents a $50,000 mistake is the best money the company spends all week; the point is knowing which one you are buying.
